He is a chemical engineer by training, who specialises in stories related to weather, climate, and the environment. Jha has been at HT since 2018, where he offers data-driven perspective and analysis on politics, environment, weather, climate, economy and society. His work includes data coverage of elections in India and abroad, including the 2019 and 2024 Lok Sabha elections; the disasters and extreme weather resulting from changing climate, such as floods, droughts, heat waves, cold waves, and dwindling snow cap in the Himalayas; the factors that drive poor air quality in northern India; the changing patterns of land use; the Covid-19 pandemic and its impact on labour market conditions; the changing pattern of consumer spending seen in the new consumer spending surveys; and social norms seen in the surveys such as the National Family Health Survey.Read More

title: A father, mother and son: Three lives lost on Maharashtra hilltop over mobile phone row
content:
A father, mother and son: Three lives lost on Maharashtra hilltop over mobile phone row
The man's father fell to his death in an attempt to save him and his mother jumped after seeing the two fall, police said
A 19-year-old man died by suicide after jumping from a hilltop in Maharashtra’s Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district on Friday afternoon, while his father also fell to his death in an attempt to save him and his mother jumped after seeing the two fall, police said.
The incident took place at Khawadya Hill in the Tisgaon area under Waluj MIDC police station.
According to police, the teenager went to the hill around 10 am after an argument with his parents over his demand for a new mobile phone. Worried about him, his parents followed him to the hilltop and tried to persuade him to return home, police said.
Deep Dive
ALSO READ: Maharashtra RTO offices begin drive to check auto, taxi drivers’ Marathi knowledge
Police, fire brigade personnel and villagers also reached the spot after receiving information that the teenager was attempting to die by suicide. Rescue personnel tried to place a safety net at the foothill, but the 19-year-old repeatedly changed his position near the edge, making it difficult for them to anticipate where he might jump, they said.
“It seems he was deliberately attempting to take the extreme step. The situation continued for nearly three hours. After 1 pm, his father slowly approached him and pleaded with him to step away from the edge. The teenager suddenly jumped, and his father also fell while trying to grab and save him,” Rameshwar Gade, inspector at Waluj MIDC police station
Seeing her husband and son fall, the mother too jumped from the hilltop, Gade added.
The inspector said the police had made extensive rescue arrangements at the spot. “Physically attempting to restrain the teenager could also have endangered the lives of police personnel,” he said.
Sanjay Jadhav, former sarpanch of Tisgaon village, who was among those trying to persuade the 19-year-old, said, “We, along with the administration, were trying to convince the teenager for almost three hours, but he was not in a condition to listen to anybody.”
Police said the bodies were recovered and were sent for further formalities.
Discussing suicides can be triggering for some. However, suicides are preventable. A few major suicide prevention helpline numbers in India are 011-23389090 from Sumaitri (Delhi-based) and 044-24640050 from Sneha Foundation (Chennai-based).

title: Bengal's new world order, 100 days on
content:
Bengal's new world order, 100 days on
After scoring the most pivotal run in years, the BJP is attempting a fundamental shift in Bengal's party society model.
Under big yellow block lettering, a group of men lumber around a shed next to a blue ice cream freezer and orange campaign posters bearing the lotus emblem. Behind them is the exposed engine of a lorry, framed by half-raised yellow shutters and contact numbers. Raw concrete pillars and scaffolding support an unplastered second storey. Below, broad bands of saffron, white, and green cover the ground floor. Small saffron flags hang from the railing, echoing the lotus motif.
Off Diamond Harbour Road near the southernmost tip of Bengal, the venue for the gathering one scorching July morning might be humble, but the purpose is anything but. Around 200 people, mandal and block-level spokespersons and leaders of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), have gathered for a daylong session. The Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Prasikhsan Maha Abhiyan 2026 is running such workshops in every block in West Bengal, especially where the BJP barely had a presence before this summer’s assembly elections.
The anchor is a 54-page booklet, printed by the BJP in Delhi, seen by HT, and translated into regional languages nationwide – Bengali here. Old-time BJP workers, fresh recruits, 20-something men with smartphones, women self-help leaders, panchayat turncoats and schoolteachers jostle for space as state-level leaders instruct them on social media campaigns, signature drives, membership logs and monthly programmes. In hour-long sessions, attendees learn how to expand booth presence, whom to target for recruitment – new voters, rickshaw pullers, daily labourers, hawkers, working women – how to field tough questions on corruption, what to post online, and how long a reel should run.
“Those who receive the training here will return to their zones and hold mandal-wise camps for booth presidents and other ground level leaders,” said Soumen Patra, a BJP leader from Diamond Harbour. “The target is that outsiders and TMC elements cannot infiltrate our ranks and claim to be our workers.”
It is a mission the BJP has only partly succeeded at. Days after sweeping to power, the party declared it would not allow indiscriminate new membership, an attempt to firewall itself against an avalanche of former Trinamool Congress leaders. Yet on the streets, in auto stands and rickshaw unions, college politics, Durga Puja committees and Bengali cinema unions, men and women have swapped the TMC’s twin flowers for the saffron flag overnight, trying to rule their petty fiefs with the same iron hand.
Also Read I ‘Pleaded with her’: Amit Shah slams Mamata Banerjee over border land delay
What is happening on the other side is unprecedented in independent India’s history. The Opposition is splintered into three groups – 20 former TMC parliamentarians who have joined the little-known Nationalist Citizens Party of India, another 62 TMC legislators who have formed a separate grouping, and a hapless Mamata Banerjee trying to keep her flock together but aware that her still-considerable popularity isn’t enough to win new followers yet. At least 90 former TMC lawmakers and panchayat leaders, Banerjee among them, have had eggs and mud hurled at them since the election.
Under the weight of expectation after a historic victory, the BJP has charted a careful course, with chief minister Suvendu Adhikari underlining transparency and industrialisation – areas where his predecessor slipped. But in a state where the party system – under the Left for 34 years, then TMC for 15 – has percolated into everyday life and every arm of government, the party is attempting to assert the supremacy of government instead, 100 days in. And in this churn, this has also reshaped what words like Hindu, refugee and citizenship mean for the state. HT takes stock.
Falta’s fallen strongman
A black SUV, its windows shattered, stands outside a hulking white two-storey compound beside a pond, its surface a blanket of green algae. The plastered walls of the house are shorn of paint, the iron gate mutilated, long scorch marks bearing scars of repeated mob outrage. Pasted next to the gate is a West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co Ltd notice claiming a pending bill of ₹3,23,956.
This is the house of Jahangir Khan, a former strongman of the TMC in Falta’s Srirampur village, around 50km south of Kolkata. “Both Khan and his wife Regina Bibi have been arrested; their two sons have fled and the house is now under lock and key,” said Imtiyaz Ali, a neighbour.
The house towers above the modest hutments and one-storey dwellings around it, expanding in fits and bursts – in tandem with Khan’s swelling power over the past decade. “He was just the son of a small local businessman but he had the blessings of the almighty number 2,” said a neighbour, referring to TMC general secretary Abhishek Banerjee.
Khan’s fief represented what scholar Dwaipayan Bhattacharya called party society, the party organisation woven into the texture of everyday life in Bengal. No place exemplifies this more than the former industrial hub of Falta, which changed hands from the Left Front to the TMC in 2011.
Ringed by rice fields on the banks of the Hoogly, the region’s roughly 220,000 residents saw everyday life shaped by the diktat of the local TMC office; those who aligned with Khan and his gang were rewarded with welfare schemes, cash doles, prime stall locations, a compliant police force, easy access to open new organisations or register businesses with dubious documents, and seats on plum quasi-government committees and Durga Puja organisations.
“Khan’s boys ran youth clubs that held blood donation camps, sports meets, and wedding bookings. Anyone building a house or repairing a wall had to purchase sand, bricks and cement from Khan-approved outlets. If someone brought outside materials, local party youth stopped the trucks or levied a fee,” said local resident Sreelata Haldar.
Penalties were reserved for those who wouldn’t fly the twin-flower flag or offer their walls for electioneering, or who approached the police instead of the party office. A senior police official admitted, on condition of anonymity, that before the May 4 results, the local station would largely ignore complaints against TMC-linked people or refer them to the party office informally.
Also Read I Bengal court issues arrest warrant against TMC MP Mahua Moitra in hate speech case
Many villagers – especially Khan’s erstwhile neighbours – refused to speak openly, aware of recriminations and alert that many former TMC associates were already crossing the ideological divide.
“This is a place where operating a toto [e-rickshaw] would need the driver to pay line money to the party union and roadside hawkers had to pay fees to the party samiti for permission to stand on the road or footpath. You think it’ll evaporate in two months?” asked an elderly man.
Left leader Sambhu Nath Kurmi, who came second in the Falta bypoll, agreed.
“There was no law and order. Whether the police or the DM, BDO, it was under Khan’s control. Things have changed now. But all grassroots TMC boys lined up to go to the BJP overnight. Does the BJP have booth workers here? All protests against TMC here are done by the new BJP men,” he said.
The former TMC fortress – the pinnacle of Abhishek Banerjee’s so-called Diamond Harbour model – is turning saffron. Most TMC leaders are in hiding or arrested. BJP flags flutter along the highway; banners of Suvendu Adhikari, Narendra Modi and Amit Shah line the road. The TMC party office has been ransacked and set ablaze more than once, leaving behind charred flags and banners.
“More than 100 TMC leaders and workers in Falta have been arrested since the results on charges of extortion, cheating, fraud, intimidating villagers and the 2021 post-poll clashes. Many have gone into hiding,” said a police officer.
A little-known party
Two lanes off the Calcutta high court stands an imposing but shabby 19th century building, its interior a maze of tiny, windowless single-desk cubicles partitioned with plywood, tin and faded wooden screens. Soot-stained walls, peeling plaster, creaky staircases, piled garbage and dangling wires fill this, home to hundreds of practising lawyers. One of them, however, is also the founder of what might become India’s fifth-largest political party by parliamentary strength.
Shewly Kundu, 39, grew up in a hamlet in border district Nadia and completed her LLB after marrying social worker Uttiya Kundu. “We didn’t have much but both my brother and I were studious. My uncle was in the RSS and father in the local BJP so we had that connect from childhood,” she said.
She began her practice in 2022, two years after her law degree. On October 13 that year, she took out an ad in newspapers, according to the requirements for registering as a recognised unregistered political party. The office of NCPI was listed at Hatgacha village in Howrah district, Saikat Das – software engineer-turned-businessman – as general secretary, and Sudam Jetty – an electronics trader – as treasurer.
In 2022-23, NCPI received ₹1,13,075 in “donations from well-wishers”. Its expenditure was almost identical, ₹1.135 lakh, including ₹49,400 on the 2023 Tripura assembly polls, per ECI records. Among the nine contributors were Kundu and vice-president Uttiya Kundu, who gave ₹15,000 and ₹18,000 respectively. The party closed the year with a balance of ₹75. No report was found for 2023-24 and 2024-25.
“We started building our social organisation around 2020. From my own funds, we built a self-help group of around 1 lakh women in Sankrail, distributed sarees and helped them get jobs,” she said.
The party’s first electoral foray was bumpy. In Tripura, the party fielded three candidates in the assembly elections. The most votes went to Chawamanu candidate Barjeda Tripura, who polled 536 votes, narrowly beating NOTA. Kundu claimed her party wasn’t allowed to field candidates in the 2023 Bengal local polls in Sankrail and Nadia.
“It was only after the state panchayat polls in 2023 that we decided to lend our full support to the BJP. We campaigned all out, organising meetings door-to-door. Many of our members had BJP-RSS backgrounds,” she said.
An NCPI leader said the party had been in touch with central and state BJP leaders since 2024, though the TMC dismissed it as small fry. “But the coordination with the BJP grew as 2026 came closer. We were part of the RSS groundwork. It is on the instructions of the BJP that Kundu resigned in June before the TMC MPs jumped ship. Many meetings happened before that,” said this leader, requesting anonymity.
Despite bursting onto the national stage two months ago, NCPI remains shrouded in mystery. Dey says Kundu never consulted him on the new joinees; Kundu says Dey never took primary membership. Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar announced in July that Jyotiprakash Chatterjee would be the new NCPI chief, but he hasn’t made a public appearance since. It remains unclear what NCPI’s plans are.
“It is not just MPs but even legislators and councillors who are in touch with us. BJP leaders from Delhi and the rebel TMC MPs are in constant touch with us. There will be more surprises in the future,” said the NCPI leader cited above.
The biggest mystery is Kundu’s elusive husband, a self-described Bengali newspaper editor, owner, publisher, mathematics teacher, motivational speaker, auditor, health consultant and yoga volunteer. His stated qualifications include an “MSc in Mathematics” along with diplomas in yoga, technical courses and land surveying.
A narrow unpaved bylane in Howrah’s Sankrail town, around 20 km from Kolkata, leads to a two-storey house painted green and saffron, with an unkempt garden. This is the registered address of both NCPI and Uttiya’s newspaper, Jago Biswa. Uttiya – who remains vice-president of NCPI – has stayed away from the media; his social media posting is prolific.
“I am not stone but water,
I stay as I am placed.
I don’t break—I adapt,” is his descriptor on Facebook.
Also Read I 100 Days of Change in West Bengal
Many of his posts riff on bite-sized philosophy – be simple, not cheap – but he has prominently posted photographs with Adhikari, and criticism of Banerjee. His most popular posts, though, are on love, pain, anger, and the frailty of human nature, each accompanied by an AI-generated poster of himself.
“In days of joy, the world is bright,
With friends around in golden light.
But hidden then, it stays away,
Waiting for a darker day.
When shadows fall and crowds depart,
And loneliness surrounds your heart,
No hand is there to hold you tight,
Through the silence of the night.
Yet gently falling down your cheek,
It speaks the words you cannot speak.
The truest friend that will appear,
Is nothing but your silent tear.”
Grassroots churn
For more than half a century, Bengal’s politics has identified itself in opposition to the national mainstream, depriving the state’s ruler of central patronage and revenue. In a populous, largely rural state with few potent axes of mobilisation, the Left made land and resource distribution its emotive issue, using rural units as instruments of control – not just for elections but everyday life and sociocultural goals. Panchayat bodies were up and running decades before the 1993 reforms that operationalised panchayati raj nationwide, and the Left used that head start to entrench its hold over the electorate. As Bengal sank into financial quicksand, these bodies grew more important in distributing largesse and securing votes. Holding the countryside laid the foundation for power. When the Left wobbled after Singur and Nandigram, it lost the panchayats first.
When Banerjee swept to power in 2011, the Left’s iron grip gave way to her personal popularity as the new glue. Left-era goons and strongmen morphed into middlemen for builders, contractors, transporters and fishery owners, coalescing around Banerjee’s brand and using extortion to grease a financial machinery that shielded them from the law – an arrangement Bhattacharya calls franchisee politics. By the evening of May 4, this model was coming apart.
Near Gariahat in south Kolkata, Bablu Mondal had taken the twin-flower flag off his auto and stand, replacing it with a saffron flag. “We couldn’t get a BJP flag because they were all sold out. We put a plain flag in the evening and changed it the next day,” he said. “Our union leader also switched sides because his dada, the councillor, left TMC.”
Having burnt its fingers with TMC turncoats in 2021, the BJP was quick to say its doors were closed to new entrants from the party. But that hasn’t stopped the migration of grassroots operatives – bus unions, conductors, auto, taxi and rickshaw operators, mill and factory workers, tea garden and coal belt unions, railway workers and porter unions, and contract worker groups. Across Kolkata, stands now display the BJP flag and many men continue to run petty local rackets, extracting money from contractors and shops – with a different garb this time.
At Howrah station, porter Rajbir Sahu had hoped his weekly “voluntary” contribution to the union dada would stop. “But he put on a gerua [saffron] cap the next day and said he was always sanatani,” he said. Clips of men misbehaving in public while claiming to be BJP leaders now rival, in number, videos of TMC leaders being chased and egged. The switches became so galling that BJP lawmaker Jitendra Tewari said publicly that extortion had doubled under the new regime, and state unit chief Samik Bhattacharya twice warned of action against those extorting money using the BJP’s name – admitting his own name was used once.
This is a strange dichotomy. Just this week, two men claiming to be youth BJP members beat up staff at a famous Kolkata sweetshop over a service complaint – but the party insists these aren’t genuine leaders. It might be technically correct, but in a state with no strong farm, caste or linguistic associations, party affiliation – official or perceived – remains the sole ladder to power. Hence, despite explicit diktats to the contrary, BJP leaders have replaced TMC leaders atop prominent puja committees, the ABVP has expanded its college-union presence fourfold in three months, and BJP-backed associations are attempting to take over the Bengali film industry and the Kolkata Book Fair, the biggest date on the Bengali cultural calendar.
Party society, reborn
Over the past 100 days, the BJP has tried to push Bengal from a party society to what Bhattacharya now calls a command society – a mirror image of Uttar Pradesh: a strongman chief minister, a controversial-but-popular law against organised crime, bulldozer action against alleged encroachers, big-ticket infra projects, and a government moving away from negotiation (what detractors call appeasement) to assert muscular dominance. The party and government remain popular; the scars of TMC excess are fresh, though some discontent is bubbling internally over rewarding turncoats and the proliferation of “good” TMC leaders.
In a landscape without an effective Opposition – Banerjee has no lieutenants, and leader of the Opposition Ritabrata Banerjee is a first-time MLA with little statewide pull – the BJP has delivered on many headline poll promises, secured the border and implemented central schemes, notwithstanding hitches with the Annapurna cash transfer scheme, whose complicated 12-page form and sub-clauses have shrunk the pool of beneficiaries.
Adhikari is set to introduce a Uniform Civil Code in a state that opposed it for 50 years. Demolished station-side stalls, a shifted Eid prayer venue and stray communal comments – all coming months after the most polarised election Bengal has seen in decades – haven’t dented this popularity. “The appeasement had to stop. Even in Park Circus, those people have to obey the law. Helmet-less motorbike hooligans used to run amok and Mamata’s police didn’t do anything. Now it’s all quiet. Suvendu has shown those people their place. This is why we voted for the BJP,” said Pratik Biswas, a Kolkata resident.
For a party battling anti-incumbency headwinds in the Hindi heartland, Bengal is a welcome breeze. But not all is well. Spiralling clashes at Jadavpur University this week triggered widespread criticism of the ABVP and belied claims that the new regime will remove politics from the campus. Three districts were paralysed as hundreds of women blocked roads and railways over being denied money under the Annapurna Yojana and its onerous conditions. And job protests have sporadically roiled Kolkata.
But on one count, the BJP’s policies might prove more consequential than anyone imagined – citizenship.
Erased from the rolls
The clump of huts where Johara Khatun lives stands in the shadow of striking Gothic palaces built by 19th century zamindars in North 24 Parganas’ Dhanyakuria hamlet. Rice fields ring this village of Nehalpur, bisected by a narrow paved road that touches all three palaces before looping back. It has been three years since Khatun, 26, was married into the village. Her husband, Ruhul, is caring, but married life has been anything but smooth.
“When the SIR was conducted, they told me that my father’s name didn’t match. But his name was there in the 2002 roll. I filled up the affidavit that the BLO gave me but they still rejected me. I filled the logical discrepancy appeal form both online and offline. But I have yet to hear from them,” she said, a sheaf of documents peeking from a scratched plastic file in her hand.
Moslem Mondal, 60, offered his own blue packet of papers. Mondal, along with his two sons Habibul and Mahabul, was removed by SIR; their appeal is pending before the Supreme Court-mandated judicial tribunal.
“We are poor villagers who have been living here for generations. But ever since our names were deleted, we have been spending sleepless nights. Already we have spent a few thousand rupees on photocopies. The man at the local computer centre charges ₹150 for each form, and we had to pay him eight times,” said Mondal.
Khatun and Mondal are among 2.71 million people removed from the electoral roll under a disputed “logical discrepancy” category, their appeals still pending before slow-moving tribunals.
Also Read I Did SIR exercise win West Bengal for the BJP?
Last week, the Supreme Court ordered a performance appraisal of the 19 tribunals – housed on Kolkata’s eastern fringes – after finding the Election Commission had no hard data on their functioning. Earlier this year, the Calcutta high court noted that at the current pace, clearing the backlog would take 21 years.
“Several cases come to us with names pending before the tribunals. I received around 13–14 such applications from Birbhum, all Muslim. It will cost ₹15,000 to file a case in the high court. Most backed out because of the financial constraints. I could file only one case,” said Kishore Mukherjee, an advocate in the Calcutta high court.
Most tribunals aren’t functioning at full capacity, listing double-digit appeals a day and winding up before the afternoon, said an official. The top court has intervened in only a handful of cases.
“I had moved the Supreme Court challenging the legality of the adjudication process and the appellate tribunals. Even my name was struck off. The Supreme Court disposed of the petition by directing the appellate tribunal to expeditiously clear my name,” said Md Yean Ali, a 75-year-old advocate from Murshidabad.
In Nehalpur, panic has mounted since the state government announced that people excluded by the SIR wouldn’t be eligible for welfare schemes, including cash doles. “I didn’t even apply. Everyone told me I wouldn’t get it,” said Khatun. “But I am scared of being called Bangladeshi.”
Roughly 30km away in Tentulia, on the edge of the international border, the state government has commandeered a guest house, Pather Sathi, into a makeshift holding centre for Bangladeshi citizens. Thirteen such centres dot the eight border districts, where suspected undocumented migrants are detained for up to five days before being controversially pushed across the border. Tentulia’s is the largest in the district.
“At present, there are around 200 illegal immigrants. They are kept in the holding centre before being handed over to the BSF to be sent across the border. They are mostly families with men, women and children. A doctor and two nurses are present during the day. They are served three simple meals but not allowed to go out,” said a police official.
A robust anti-migrant stance is at the core of Adhikari’s tough administrator image, sitting uneasily with the BJP’s new strategy of lionising Partition as an event that saved Bengali Hindus, in contrast with its rhetoric elsewhere in the country blaming the Congress for Partition. But in Nehalpur, the uncertainty of citizenship and the vitriol of being branded Bangladeshi makes for a bitter cocktail.
“I had around ₹37,000 in the bank. As panic gripped the villager and rumours grew, everyone told me that I could be branded a Bangladeshi and my account could be frozen. I withdrew the entire amount and kept it in my house,” said Ansar Mondal, 59.
Also Read I SIR exercise: 1 lakh plus voters flagged for scrutiny, 67% served notices so far in Chandigarh
Arman Gazi wondered why his name and his elder brother’s were left off the rolls while his parents made it. Anju Khatun – who has seven siblings – was flagged because her father was connected to more than six people. Julie Khatun couldn’t prove her name was misspelled on the rolls. “I gave documents of my mother and father, Aadhaar, Madhyamik (Class 10) pass certificate, admit card, but nothing worked. I worry what if they cancel my ration card,” she said.
Johara Khatun is more sanguine. She is clear the chances of receiving the Annapurna money are bleak, as is getting enrolled in any new scheme; her family has promised to divide the dole. But she is still waiting on that call from the local dada about her appeal.
“I went to every camp organised here that taught us how to fill the forms, but failed. Maybe it is my fault that I am illiterate. But I didn’t come from anywhere else, I am Indian,” she said. “Please believe me.”

title: NIA raids 10 locations across Jammu and Kashmir in cross-border terror conspiracy case
content:
INDIA
The raids were carried out in Srinagar, Kupwara, Anantnag, Pulwama, and Budgam districts of Jammu and Kashmir.
The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Saturday conducted searches at 10 locations across Jammu and Kashmir in connection with the investigation of a cross-border terror conspiracy involving Pak-based handlers and a network of local Over Ground Workers (OGWs) allegedly providing logistical and other forms of support to infiltrated terrorists.
The raids were carried out in Srinagar, Kupwara, Anantnag, Pulwama and Budgam districts in Jammu and Kashmir. As per the anti-terror agency, the searches were aimed at securing further documentary, digital and material evidence relating to the conspiracy and at ascertaining the roles of persons allegedly associated with the local support network.
The case, arising out of FIR No. 0024/2026 of Zakoora Police Station in Srinagar, was subsequently re-registered by the NIA this year under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, the Arms Act, 1959, and Explosive Substances Act, 1908. The case was initiated following the arrest of an OGW allegedly associated with the proscribed terrorist organisation Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) during the late-night hours of March 31, at a naka point, from whose possession a hand grenade and live ammunition were recovered. During the investigation, Pakistani terrorists allegedly connected with the conspiracy were arrested, and the identities and alleged roles of members of the local support network were also ascertained.
"Investigation conducted so far has indicated alleged linkages between Pak-based handlers and local associates, who were allegedly being used for communication, logistical arrangements, movement and concealment of terrorists, provision of shelter, reconnaissance and other forms of facilitation," said the NIA in a statement.
The investigation is also examining the financial trail, communication channels, movement of the accused, and the source of arms and explosives, with a view to establishing the complete network and the extent of its activities. NIA said the searches conducted on Saturday were part of its continuing investigation into the larger conspiracy and the alleged facilitation mechanism supporting cross-border terrorism. "Further evidence relevant to the investigation has been secured and is being examined and corroborated with other material collected in the case," it added.
The Central agency further said it is continuing its investigation to identify all persons involved and ascertain their respective roles in the conspiracy, and that further legal action, including arrests or recoveries, may follow, subject to the outcome of the investigation.
(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by DNA staff and is published from news agency ANI).

title: 'India's biggest strength': Rahul Gandhi lauds women at Chhatron Ki Goonj event in Pune
content:
INDIA
Gandhi said that women are naturally more sensitive, gentle, compassionate, and forward-looking, making them fundamental to the nation's progress.
Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi on Saturday highlighted the potential of women in the country, emphasising that India's true strength lies in its citizens, particularly its women's population, while addressing the Congress party's Pune leg of 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' campaign here.
The Congress MP shared his views on women's rights, societal perceptions, and India's core strengths. "Many times, people ask me, 'What is India's biggest strength?' You get many answers when you ask this question. Somebody will say our economy. Somebody will say our military. Somebody will say our medical system. Somebody might even say our people, but I am very clear on what is India's biggest strength, our biggest asset, and that strength is 70 crore unique journeys, unique imaginations, unique dreams that the women of India are living," he said.
Gandhi added that women are naturally more sensitive, gentle, compassionate, and forward-looking, making them fundamental to the nation's progress. Further, he critiqued how society often restricts women to limited roles, ignoring their diverse professional and personal achievements. "Whenever I speak to a man, women are put in three boxes. You are seen as a daughter, a wife, or a mother. Now, there is nothing wrong with being seen as a wife, daughter, or mother. But this cannot be your only identity," he said.
He reiterated that the women excelling in various domains must realise that being someone's wife, daughter, or mother is not their entire identity. He added that they deserve recognition far beyond these traditional societal limitations. "It cannot be that we have brilliant women who are doing completely fascinating and different things, who are professionals, who are sportswomen, who do multiple different things, and then the only identity that they are given by our men is these three," he added.
Gandhi quoted ancient texts to underscore the alleged historical barriers placed on female independence. "The Manusmriti says that ' in childhood, a female belongs to her father. In youth, she belongs to her husband. When her lord is dead, she belongs to her sons. A woman must never be independent.' This is a direct quote from the Manusmriti, and these words are a shame, because these words should never ever have been spoken," he alleged.
Rahul Gandhi launched 'Chhatron Ki Goonj', a nationwide student-led political campaign in mid-2026. The movement aims to be a national platform for student grievances in education and recruitment, such as exam irregularities, paper leaks, rising fees, privatisation of higher education, and unemployment linked to corruption in competitive recruitment. The campaign demands equal job opportunities and greater structural safety for aspirants. Earlier, the Chhatron ki Goonj campaign was held in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh on August 8. Prior to that, Gandhi took the campaign to Dehradun, Uttarakhand on July 17. The first leg of the campaign was held in Kota, Rajasthan, on June 17.
(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by DNA staff and is published from news agency ANI).

title: Maharashtra: CJP Chief Abhijeet Dipke booked for entering Latur govt school without permission
content:
INDIA
Cockroach Janta Party convenor Abhijeet Dipke booked with Ajinkya Shinde & others in Latur for entering ZP Urdu school in Jawali near Ausa without permission, disrupting work, threatening teachers.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) convenor Abhijeet Dipke was booked along with others in Maharashtra's Latur for allegedly entering a government school without permission. A First Information Report (FIR) was registered against Dipke, party worker Ajinkya Shinde and other CJP workers at Ausa police station.
They have been accused of disrupting official work and threatening teachers at ZP Urdu school at Jawali near Ausa, a city in Latur district.
The FIR was registered after a teacher at a Zilla Parishad Urdu school, Sayyed Shamshadbano Khairatali (53), filed a complaint.
Dipke and the others have been booked under BNS sections 132 (Assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty), 329(3) (house trespass), 351(2) (criminal intimidation) and 356(2) (criminal defamation).
According to the FIR, Dipke and his associates have been accused of entering the school premises without permission from the authorities. They reportedly sat with students and raised questions about the conditions of the school. The complaint alleged that they were causing obstruction to educational and government work.
The CJP leader also recorded videos of their visit and interaction with students and posted it on social media, the complaint said.
Dipke allegedly tried to defame the ZP Urdu school as he claimed that students from another school were brought and made to sit in the classrooms during his visit. He also threatened to get the teachers suspended, it alleged.
The Cockroach Janta Party members have been visiting government-run schools, under their 'School Thik Karo' campaign, which was launched on the country's Independence Day, August 15.
The programme, which seeks to reform education and amenities in government schools across the country, was started from Dipke's native village in Hingoli. Since then the CJP members have visited several schools in different states, while also facing opposition in some.
A CJP team was allegedly attacked by the people while visiting a government school in Jaipur's Rampura Kanwarpura on Friday.
In Mumbai, the civic education department has barred volunteers of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) from entering municipal schools without permission.
Police said further investigation is underway.

title: Bar Council chairman Manan Mishra rejects allegations against him: 'It's all a political stunt'
content:
INDIA
Responding to the allegations leveled by senior advocate YR Sadasiva Reddy, Mishra said he was an elected representative and not a nominated member of the BCI.
Bar Council of India (BCI) Chairman and BJP MP Manan Kumar Mishra has responded to allegations raised by BCI member and senior advocate YR Sadasiva Reddy, who has demanded Mishra's resignation and sought an independent inquiry into the functioning of the statutory body. Responding to the allegations and a letter written by Reddy, Mishra said he was an elected representative and not a nominated member of the BCI. "I am an elected representative. I was neither selected nor nominated to the Bar Council of India. It is a statutory body established under the Advocates Act. Over 2.5 million lawyers across the country are voters in this system," Mishra said.
On Reddy's claim of being the BCI Co-Chairman, Mishra said, "First of all, I must clarify that he is not a Co-Chairman of the Bar Council of India. Rather, today, he is not even a member of the State Bar Council. Number two, it's a democratic body. People are elected."
Mishra alleged that Reddy's criticism was politically motivated and said there was internal and party politics within the organisation. "There are groups, and there is internal politics as well as party politics. He belongs to another political party and normally supports Congress members. Therefore, it's all a political vendetta and a political stunt," Mishra said. He further alleged that Reddy had remained silent during his earlier tenure as a BCI member. "He has been a member of the Bar Council of India for the last eight and a half years. But throughout those eight and a half years, he has never opened his mouth," Mishra said.
Responding to allegations concerning a trust, Mishra said Reddy himself was a trustee of the organisation. "Now he is talking about a trust of which he himself is a trustee. Therefore, these baseless allegations levelled by Mr Reddy have no meaning at all. He has no concern with the Bar Council of India today," Mishra said. "The Bar Council of India is still a very strong institution, and it will be a very strong institution in the future as well. Therefore, whatever a man like Reddy or ABCD may say, it has no value at all," he added.
Mishra also explained the process through which the BCI Chairman is elected. "First, they elect their representatives to the State Bar Council. The representatives from all State Bar Councils then elect their representatives to the Bar Council of India, and collectively, these representatives from all states elect the Chairman and Vice-Chairman," he said. On his long tenure as BCI Chairman, Mishra said, "This is my seventh term. I have been elected unopposed for the last six terms. Even today, more than two-thirds of the Bar Council members support me."
He dismissed allegations concerning a trust and the appointment of relatives, saying there was no substance to the claims. "If a handful of individuals are making baseless allegations, whether regarding a trust or the appointment of a relative, there is no substance to them. These unfounded claims are surfacing only now," Mishra said. On the functioning of the trust, Mishra said its operations were transparent and subject to annual audits. "Regarding the trust, its entire functioning is completely transparent. The managing trustees include distinguished individuals--Bar Council members and senior advocates. Anyone is welcome to examine the accounts; the trust undergoes an annual audit. The audit report is incorporated into the budget, published, and made available in the public domain," he said.
Mishra also criticised those making allegations against the BCI, alleging that some had no connection with the statutory body. "These baseless allegations are being made by a few individuals--such as those from the CJP--who have no connection to the Bar Council. They have even gone so far as to call lawyers 'legal cockroaches.' This is deeply shameful for the legal fraternity, and the community of lawyers will never tolerate such baseless and frivolous remarks," Mishra said. "Manan Mishra will remain president as long as the country's lawyers, the voters, want him to stay," he added.
Meanwhile, senior advocate and BCI member YR Sadasiva Reddy has demanded Mishra's resignation, alleging that the functioning of the statutory body has moved away from the principles of transparency and accountability. In a letter dated August 22, 2026, addressed to Mishra, Reddy called for his resignation as Chairman and sought an independent inquiry into several issues raised by him. Reddy said he was making the demand not as an adversary but as an elected BCI member and a member of the legal profession for more than three decades.
He said the BCI was a statutory body constituted under the Advocates Act, 1961, and that its powers and funds were held in trust for the benefit of the legal profession. "It is my considered view, formed on the basis of what I have myself witnessed in the meetings of this Council, that under your Chairmanship the Council has drifted very far from that standard," Reddy said in the letter.
One of the principal grounds cited by Reddy relates to appointments within the BCI establishment. He alleged that appointments had been made without a transparent recruitment process and claimed that a significant proportion of the staff comprised persons connected or related to members of the Council. Reddy said he was unable to find in the records placed before the Council any advertisement, selection committee proceedings or comparative merit list justifying such appointments. He said the issue was particularly concerning because the BCI exercises regulatory powers over the legal profession and handles funds contributed by advocates. Reddy has also called for a special meeting of the BCI to consider the issues raised by him, with relevant records to be made available to every member in advance.
Among his other demands is a special audit of the accounts of the BCI and the BCI Trust Fund from the date of their registration. He has sought that the audit be conducted by an independent firm empanelled with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India and that the report be circulated to every Council member and made public. Reddy has further sought an immediate direction that no contribution, donation or payment of any description be received from any law college, university or management by the Council or by any trust or body connected with it. He has also demanded that the complete staff position referred to in his allegations regarding appointments be uploaded on the BCI's website. Reddy said he had no personal animosity towards Mishra and pointed out that he had served alongside him on the Council for about a decade. He said his demand was based on his assessment of the functioning of the institution during that period. "There are able persons in this Council capable of restoring it," Reddy said, adding that stepping down voluntarily would allow Mishra to take credit for facilitating such a transition. The letter concludes with Reddy stating that the Bar of the country "deserves better" from its own Council and urging Mishra to allow an opportunity for the institution to be restored.
(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by DNA staff and is published from news agency ANI).

title: Stop electric shock glove plan for ICE: U.S. lawmakers  to Trump administration
content:
Indian American Congressman Shri Thanedar and two others have asked the U.S. government to immediately halt the Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) plan to procure electric shock gloves for its officers.
In a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Mr. Thanedar, the ranking member of the Congressional subcommittee on oversight, investigations and accountability, warned that using gloves capable of delivering electric shocks could be abused by ICE personnel and result in injury or death.
ICE plans to spend up to $20 million to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and agents by March.
The Department of Homeland Security described the gloves, capable of delivering painful electric shocks, as a “de-escalation device.” “Given ICE’s horrific record of violence against the public, the agency must not be allowed to equip its officers and agents with a device that demands both significant training for and restraint by its users,” Mr. Thanedar, Bennie Thompson and Lou Correa said in the letter to Mullin on Friday.
Mr. Thompson is the ranking member of the Committee on Homeland Security, while Correa and Mr. Thanedar are ranking members of the congressional subcommittees on Border Security and Enforcement, and Oversight, Investigations and Accountability, respectively.
“Under Trump, ICE has hired unqualified officers and agents and rushed them through training programs with reduced use of force instruction. Many of these officers and agents should not have been hired at all, much less let loose on American streets with a badge, a gun, and electric shock gloves,” the lawmakers said.
The Members urged Secretary Mullin to intervene and halt the procurement before it moves forward, warning that the devices could be incorrectly used or abused by ICE personnel and result in further injury or death.
ICE is facing criticism for use of aggressive tactics as it carries out President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.
ICE agents have deployed pepper spray against protestors, dragged people out of vehicles and fatally shot at least six people during Mr. Trump’s second term in office, leading to calls for greater accountability.

title: More than 20 injured as moderate earthquake shakes northeast Japan
content:
A moderate earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 5.9 rattled eastern Japan, including the Tokyo area, early Sunday (August 23, 2026), injuring more than 20 people, most of them slightly, officials said. There was no danger of a tsunami.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, the quake occurred in the southern Ibaraki prefecture, at a depth of 70 kilometres, an area of Japan prone to frequent quakes. The U.S. Geological Survey recorded a preliminary magnitude of 5.8.
Twenty-three people were injured in four prefectures in the region -- nine in Saitama, another nine in Kanagawa, four in Chiba and one in Ibaraki — according to prefectural officials.
Most of them were injured when they fell down or hit themselves against furniture or doors as they were caught off guard by the quake while sleeping and got out of bed in a panic, officials said. Among them was a woman in her 80s who fell off the bed and suffered a serious hip injury in Yokohama, in the Kanagawa prefecture, the Yomiuri newspaper reported.
The quake caused delays to express trains serving Tokyo and Narita Airport and other local trains serving northeastern regions, but Shinkansen bullet trains were running normally, their operator East Japan Railway Company said.
The government set up a task force to assess the extent of possible damage, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on X.
The temblor set off emergency quake alerts on mobile phones and also significantly shook Tokyo. NHK public television showed traffic on roads in nearby cities, including Mito and Saitama, seemingly normal.
An underground water pipe ruptured in Tokyo’s eastern ward of Koto, with water pouring out onto the road, NHK footage showed. The pipe has been repaired and the leak was stopped later. The earthquake caused blackouts to about 460 homes in Tokyo, but power was restored by later Sunday morning, according to TEPCO Power Grid.
There were no reports of anomalies from about a dozen nuclear power plants and other facilities that handle nuclear materials, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said.
Last month, a magnitude 7.1 quake struck the Kumamoto area on Japan’s southernmost island of Kyushu, killing 38 people and injuring 364. It also destroyed more than 1,500 buildings and damaged nearly 20,000 others.

title: MP hospital fire: 3 newborns suffer burn injuries after NICU warmer catches fire
content:
INDIA
Three newborns were injured after a warmer caught fire inside the NICU of Chhindwara District Hospital.
Three newborn babies suffered burn injuries after a warmer caught fire inside the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) of Chhindwara District Hospital in Madhya Pradesh, officials said.
The incident took place during the intervening night of Friday and Saturday. Considering the condition of the injured infants, doctors referred them to Jabalpur Medical College for specialised treatment.
According to reports, a sudden spark developed in the filament of the heating unit of a warmer being used inside the NICU. The machine reportedly caught fire soon after.
Three newborns were inside the warmer when the incident occurred and sustained burn injuries. Hospital staff immediately removed the infants from the machine and began providing medical assistance. The fire was also brought under control using a fire extinguisher.
Chhindwara District Hospital Civil Surgeon Kanchan Dubey said there were 33 children in the unit when the incident occurred.
"On 22nd August, 2026, at around 1.50 pm, there is a children's intensive care unit, in which the children are kept in a warmer, or the serious children are admitted for treatment. So, in one of the children's warmers, due to a sudden spark in the filament, there was a fire in that warmer, due to which three children were injured due to burning. As soon as our staff saw them, they immediately removed all three children from there, extinguished the fire with a fire extinguisher, and took out the whole burning trolley. There is an oxygen connection there, which could have been very dangerous; that was also closed."
She said the remaining babies were immediately moved to safety.
"There were 33 children in that place. 3 children were kept in a cradle, in a warmer; the remaining 30 children were safely taken out of there. After taking them out, the three children who were injured due to burning we took them to the medical college specialists. The medical superintendent, they also came immediately as soon as they got the news. They saw him, tested him, and then, for better treatment, they referred him to Medical College, Jabalpur."
The three injured infants were transported to Jabalpur by ambulance under the supervision of two doctors.
Hospital authorities said the babies were referred to Jabalpur Medical College so they could receive advanced medical treatment. The incident also raised concerns over the safety of medical equipment being used in the NICU.

title: Delhi software engineer beaten to death by in-laws after fight over child's medicine
content:
INDIA
Delhi software engineer Vinay Gupta, 31, Adobe employee with Rs 60 lakh package, allegedly beaten to death by in-laws in Nihal Vihar after fight with wife Rekha over child's medicine.
A domestic fight at a home in Delhi ended in tragedy when a 31-year-old software engineer died after he was allegedly beaten to death by his in-laws.
The incident took place this morning in Delhi's Nihal Vihar when an argument broke out between the victim, Vinay Gupta, and his wife, Rekha, over giving medicine to their child. During this time, Rekha left the house after contacting her family members, who later arrived at the couple's residence. Around 10 minutes later, she returned with her two brothers, sister-in-law, father and uncle, along with other family members.
CCTV footage from the incident showed Rekha wearing a red suit and her sister-in-law in a blue suit. The footage also purportedly showed Rekha's two brothers, her father and another man in a car.
Subsequently, they began assaulting Vinay.
According to the victim's mother - who was living with the couple - she had stepped out to arrange water and refreshments for the visitors when the alleged assault began. When she returned, she found her son being attacked. She tried to intervene and called for help, pleading with them to stop, but the assault continued, his family members said.
The victim's family said his in-laws strangled him and inflicted blows and kicks on his chest. They alleged that the attack was a part of a pre-planned conspiracy, claiming that Rekha had switched off all the CCTV cameras in the house before the incident.
Minutes after the assault, Vinay's neighbour was seen carrying him on his shoulder to take him to the hospital. Rekha's family members were also seen standing behind him. Soon, the victim was taken to a hospital where doctors declared him dead.
Vinay used to work at Adobe - a Noida-based software company - and had an annual package of around Rs 60 lakh.
He had married Rekha around three-and-a-half years ago. The couple had twins - a boy and a girl - who were born around four-and-a-half months ago.
At the Delhi home, Vinay and his wife lived on the third floor of the house, while his parents lived downstairs. According to his family, Rekha used to cook separately and alleged that her brother had earlier threatened to kill Vinay over minor disputes.
Police have arrested four people in connection with the case - Rekha, her two brothers and one sister-in-law. Further investigation is underway.

title: Hyderabad Aston Martin Crash: Preliminary drug test negative for MP's son
content:
INDIA
Preliminary alcohol and drug tests on Lingamaneni Sanjush, 21, son of AP Rajya Sabha MP Lingamaneni Ramesh, negative after fatal Aston Martin crash that killed 26-yr-old Bharati Mukhi near Inorbit Mall.
Preliminary alcohol and drug tests conducted on Lingamaneni Sanjush, 21, son of Andhra Pradesh Rajya Sabha MP Lingamaneni Ramesh, have returned negative following the fatal Aston Martin crash in Hyderabad, police said.
Sanjush was driving the luxury car when it struck 26-year-old sales executive Bharati Mukhi near Inorbit Mall on August 16. Bharati sustained critical injuries and was taken to Apollo Hospital, where she was declared dead on arrival.
According to police, Sanjush was driving at high speed and in a rash and negligent manner when the accident occurred. The luxury vehicle has since been seized and inspected by a Motor Vehicle Inspector, with the inspection report awaited.
Police have registered a case under Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which deals with causing death by a rash or negligent act and carries a maximum punishment of five years.
The Aston Martin was reportedly not registered in Sanjush's name.
Although preliminary tests for alcohol and drugs were negative, police have sent Sanjush's blood sample to the Forensic Science Laboratory for further examination. The forensic report, along with the MVI report and post-mortem findings, will form part of the ongoing investigation.
Bharati's remains were handed over to her brother following the post-mortem examination and were later taken to Odisha. The post-mortem report is also awaited.
Police said they did not find grounds for Sanjush's immediate arrest based on the material available at the time. He was instead served a notice under Section 35 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, directing him to cooperate with the investigation.
The DCP rejected claims that Sanjush was not arrested because of political or external influence. The officer said the decision was taken in accordance with legal requirements and Supreme Court guidelines.
Sanjush has said he did not flee the accident spot after the collision. He claimed he took Bharati to the hospital and subsequently cooperated with the police investigation.
Bharati, who worked as a sales executive, was reportedly the sole earning member of her family. Her death has prompted calls for financial assistance to her family as the police investigation continues.

title: Two bodies recovered, about 12 missing after migrant boat capsized off Tunisian coast
content:
A boat carrying migrants capsized off the coast of southern Tunisia, killing at least two people and leaving 12 missing, Tunisia's national guard said on Saturday (August 22, 2026). One survivor was rescued.
Guard spokesperson Houssem Eddine Jebabli told the state news agency TAP that authorities recovered two bodies and transferred them to a hospital on the nearby island of Djerba. He told national radio Mosaique FM that about 15 people were believed to be aboard the boat when it took off between the cities of Zarzis and Ben Guerdane.
The boat had set off early on Thursday (August 20), and a commercial ship found the sole survivor on Saturday (August 22) in a life jacket, Mosaique reported, citing testimony from the survivor.
A helicopter and coast guard boats were then dispatched to the area in search of more survivors, according to an Associated Press photojournalist at the scene. The migrants were believed to be headed toward Italy.
Zarzis has long been a departure point for Tunisians and others from around Africa or beyond, attempting to cross the Mediterranean toward Europe.
The city witnessed a similar tragedy in 2022, when a boat carrying 18 people went missing. The incident sparked weeks of protests as families accused authorities of failing to properly search for their relatives and burying some recovered bodies without identifying them or informing their families.
Migrant departures from Tunisia have fallen sharply since the European Union and Tunisia signed a sweeping agreement in 2023. It included EU funding and technical support for Tunisian border control and coast guard training to help Tunisia curb irregular migration and deter human traffickers in the Mediterranean basin. The EU allocated 105 million euros (USD 121 million) in migration-related support to Tunisia in 2023 alone.
The decline in migration has not ended dangerous crossings from Tunisia's southern coast, where families in the south, particularly in Zarzis, have for years searched for relatives who disappeared at sea.
Rights groups have raised concerns about the treatment of migrants and asylum seekers in Tunisia since the EU agreement, including reports of collective expulsions, racial violence, arbitrary detention and abuses against Black migrants.
In July, Amnesty International said EU support for border control in Tunisia continued to fuel serious rights violations. It said refugees and asylum seekers were being “deliberately trapped in a system that offers neither protection nor a safe way out.”

title: India slams USCIRF as biased after it seeks sanctions on RSS, says 'they have their own agenda'
content:
INDIA
India slams USCIRF as biased organisation after it urged sanctions on RSS and opposed Mohan Bhagwat's Aug 29 New York visit. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said body lacks credibility, ignores India's pluralistic framework.
India has criticised the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom for urging sanctions against the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, calling it a biased organisation.
External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the US body has been making disparaging and inflammatory remarks about India.
"It is a biased organisation. I would say that we should keep away from such organisations as they have their own agenda and lack any credibility...We do not expect that the USCIRF will engage with the reality of India's pluralistic framework or acknowledge the harmonious coexistence of its diverse communities," Jaiswal said.
USCIRF chair Asif Mahmood - a Pakistan-born American citizen who has maintained close ties with his homeland's political and diplomatic leadership - had opposed RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's upcoming visit to the US and called upon the US government to impose sanctions on the RSS. Bhagwat is scheduled to visit New York on August 29.
The US body also asked Washington not to extend diplomatic courtesies to its leaders, and described RSS as an umbrella organisation whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities.
"Instead, the USG should focus on imposing sanctions on RSS members found responsible for FoRB violations," the US body said.
Earlier in March, the USCIRF annual report criticised India for alleged violations of religious freedom and backed targeted sanctions on individuals and entities such as the RSS and Research and Analysis Wing. In its recommendation, the USCIRF also called for designating India as a country of particular concern.
The USCIRF is an independent, bipartisan US federal government agency. It makes policy recommendations to the US President, the Secretary of State, and Congress, and tracks their implementation.
A US-based advocacy group, HinduPACT, condemned the public opposition by members of the USCIRF to the RSS chief's visit to New York, saying the US body has disgraced its mandate.
"When its chair speaks about India and the RSS, he sounds less like the head of a pluralistic American commission and more like an advocate for a hardened anti-Hindu narrative...Mohan Bhagwat leads one of the world's most consequential Hindu organisations. He should not be met with slander scripted by CAIR, IAMC, and HfHR, groups that have made a habit of treating Hindu self-assertion as extremism," said Ajay Shah, Founder and Chair of HinduPACT

title: Flying abroad from India? This boarding pass rule changes from September 1
content:
INDIA
Flying out of India soon? A familiar airport process is set to disappear on September 1, as physical boarding pass stamping will no longer be required. Yes, you read it right! Know more below.
If you are planning to fly abroad from an Indian airport in the coming days, a familiar step in your airport journey is set to vanish. Yes, you read it right! Physical stamping of boarding passes will end on September 1, which will now change the way travellers have been through airports.
As per a report by ANI, officials have confirmed that passengers will no longer need to get their physical boarding passes stamped at Indian airports, which will make the process much simpler and also reduce the need for manual procedures at airports.
''E-boarding passes will also be accepted at immigration counters in addition to physical boarding passes. The stamping of boarding passes has been done away with,'' ANI reported, quoting an official.
The Bureau of Immigration (BOI), under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), has communicated the decision to airport authorities, following concerns that the current practice of physically stamping boarding passes was causing inconvenience to passengers.
This move is a part of the Centre's push towards digital and paperless airport processes.
To put it in simple words, this change will help travellers with one less step at the airport. However, passengers will still have to complete all mandatory security, immigration and other airport checks. It only removes the physical requirement of getting the boarding pass stamped.
Of course, yes, passengers will still need a valid boarding pass for their journey. The only change is that the boarding pass will no longer need the traditional physical stamp as part of the airport process.
International travellers will still have to complete the required immigration and security procedures before boarding their flights.

title: Ranchi protest escalates as students target Hemant Soren, Rahul Gandhi with effigies | Video
content:
INDIA
Students protesting alleged irregularities in Jharkhand recruitment exams clashed with police in Ranchi after they attempted to burn effigies of Hemant Soren and Rahul Gandhi.
A protest by students over alleged irregularities in Jharkhand recruitment exams turned tense in Ranchi on Friday, with protesters and police getting into a scuffle. The agitators were attempting to burn effigies of Chief Minister Hemant Soren and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi.
Members of the JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch gathered at Albert Chowk, accusing the Jharkhand government of failing job aspirants following recent developments in recruitment cases. The protest came after the Jharkhand High Court stayed notifications cancelling appointments linked to the 11th and 13th JPSC examinations and the JSSC-CGL exam.
	
#WATCH | Ranchi, Jharkhand: JPSC-JSSC aspirants to burn effigies of Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren and Lok Sabha LoP and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi as part of their ongoing protest near Albert Ekka Chowk in Ranchi
		
		A large number of police personnel are also present at the… pic.twitter.com/96zPoEYacb
According to police, the protesters were supposed to follow a designated route but changed their path and reached the JPSC office, disrupting traffic.
Lalpur police station officer-in-charge Rupesh Kumar Singh said police repeatedly asked the protesters to follow the approved route, but they did not comply.
An official said the situation turned tense when police tried to stop the protesters from burning the effigies. JMM workers were also reportedly present at the location. Student leaders, however, alleged that police and ruling Jharkhand Mukti Morcha workers tried to prevent them from carrying out a peaceful demonstration.
JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch leader Ravindra Paswan said the protesters would continue to exercise their right to hold peaceful demonstrations.
Another student leader, Piyush Kumar Singh, alleged that a core committee member named Kunal was detained during the protest and later fainted. He was subsequently taken to Sadar Hospital, he claimed.
The protesters also alleged that female participants were assaulted during the confrontation.
Similar clashes were reportedly witnessed in Hazaribag and Giridih, where JMM workers and students allegedly confronted each other over attempts to burn effigies of the chief minister. The allegations made by the protesters could not be independently verified.
Meanwhile, JLKM leader Devendra Nath Mahto announced a 'Recruitment System Reforms Yatra' beginning August 24.
Mahto accused the Jharkhand government of failing to strongly defend its position in cases related to cancelled recruitment examinations. He warned that if the government did not effectively present its case before the High Court during the September 15 hearing, protesters could consider gheraoing the chief minister's residence.
The latest developments follow a series of court orders concerning recruitment examinations in the state. On Friday, the High Court stayed notifications cancelling appointments of Child Development Project Officers and candidates recruited through the JSSC-CGL examination.
A day earlier, the court had also stayed notifications cancelling the 11th and 13th JPSC examinations and the appointments of food safety officers.

title: BJP passes resolution on Vande Mataram, condemns Congress' stance on national song
content:
INDIA
The BJP strongly condemned the Congress Working Committee's decision taken on August 19 to re-adopt its 1937 resolution that restricts the singing of Vande Mataram to only its first two stanzas at Congress programmes.
The Bharatiya Janata Party on Saturday passed a major resolution on the honour and historic legacy of 'Vande Mataram' and said that it will lead a nationwide campaign to raise awareness around the history and significance of the National song. The party strongly condemned the Congress Working Committee's decision taken on August 19 to re-adopt its 1937 resolution that restricts the singing of Vande Mataram to only its first two stanzas at Congress programmes.
The BJP said it considers Vande Mataram as India's National Song, an expression of reverence for Bharat Mata, the mantra of the freedom struggle and the immortal symbol of India's national consciousness. BJP's resolution mentioned that the party will strongly oppose the Congress decision to limit Vande Mataram to two stanzas. It will protect the honour, dignity and legacy of the full six-stanza Vande Mataram. It will reaffirm the 1950 Constituent Assembly declaration and the law passed by Parliament in 2026 giving statutory protection to the National Song at par with Jana Gana Mana.
It will oppose any attempt to make the National Song subservient to communal pressure, appeasement or vote-bank politics. The resolution emphasised that Congress's Working Committee resolution cannot be above the Constitution and Parliament's law. The political compromise of 1937 cannot override the constitutional decision of 1950 and the 2026 law.
The resolution said the party will bring before the public the historical context behind restricting Vande Mataram, including objections by the Muslim League and the politics of communal and separatist demands. It will take Mahatma Gandhi's statement to the masses, where he had described Vande Mataram as an "anti-imperialist slogan" linked to the "purest national sentiment."
BJP workers will run a nationwide campaign to take the history, meaning and national importance of Vande Mataram to every corner of the country. A special awareness drive will be held among the youth so that the full National Song is not forgotten and future generations understand its deep link with India's freedom, struggle and sacrifice. No compromise on Vande Mataram's honour will be accepted for political convenience, the resolution said.
The BJP said this is not just about a political party, but about India's honour and the legacy of countless patriots who sacrificed everything for the nation. The words of Vande Mataram were once so powerful that an empire was terrified of them. The British tried to suppress them because they awakened resistance. Generations adopted them as a mantra of freedom and national pride. This legacy cannot be reduced to vote-bank arithmetic, the resolution said.
In 1947, the clarion call of India's independence was 'Vande Mataram', and under PM Narendra Modi, the grand proclamation of 'Viksit Bharat' in 2047 will also be 'Vande Mataram'. On Wednesday, the Congress Working Committee also decided that only the first two stanzas of the national song would be sung at party events, citing the party's own 1937 resolution.
The decision followed days of controversy after the BJP accused Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and party parliamentary chairperson Sonia Gandhi of conversing while the national song was being rendered during Independence Day celebrations on August 15, and demanded a public apology. After the CWC meeting, Congress MP KC Venugopal said the party's stand on the recitation of Vande Mataram was clear and that it would follow the decisions taken by Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel in 1937.
(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by DNA staff and is published from news agency ANI).

title: Nancy Kassebaum Baker, former U.S. senator from Kansas, dies at 94
content:
Nancy Kassebaum Baker, a Kansas governor's daughter who became the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without following a spouse into office, has died. She was 94.
Kassebaum Baker died Friday (August 21, 2026) of natural causes, according to her son, Bill Kassebaum.
“She loved Kansas. She loved people from Kansas and represented Kansas for 18 years in the US Senate,” he told The Associated Press. “She was an independent-minded Republican who was willing to stand up for what she thought was right, even if that meant going against the party.”
She was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1978 and served three terms. Her modest demeanour endeared her to voters of all political stripes, though she shared the moderate, progressive Republican politics of her father, Gov. Alf Landon, the unsuccessful 1936 GOP nominee for president. Even after leaving the Senate early in 1997, she continued taking on public service roles.
She married former Senator Howard Baker, a Tennessee Republican, in 1996. He died in 2014.
Kassebaum Baker remained an icon for Kansans generally. She could work with Senate colleagues of all political philosophies, and a 1996 health insurance law bore her name, along with that of liberal Massachusetts Senator Ted Kennedy.
A centrist politician from America's heartland
Her election to the Senate brought her immediate national attention. When she announced her retirement, she was among eight women senators and the only one to chair a Senate committee, the Labour and Human Resources panel.
She was also in a dwindling bloc of moderate-to-liberal Republicans, having supported for example a ban on assault weapons championed by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat.
Yet she never polarised Kansas conservatives as other GOP moderates did. She connected with voters because she never seemed caught up in the trappings of power, and when she retired, she acknowledged, “I'd rather cuddle up and do needlepoint all day.”
She was born on July 29, 1932, as her father, an oilman from Independence, was running for the first of his two terms as governor. She earned a political science degree from the University of Kansas and a master's degree in diplomatic history from the University of Michigan in the mid-1950s.
She was a radio-station executive, spent a year in the 1970s on the staff of Kansas Sen. James Pearson and served on the school board in the Wichita suburb of Maize. She had four children with her first husband, Phil Kassebaum, including Bill, who served a term in the Kansas House. The marriage ended in divorce in 1979.
A moderate who sought sensible solutions
When Kassebaum Baker decided to run for the U.S. Senate, she figured that “a woman with a background different from a man might be appealing” to people growing weary of politics. Pundits at the time estimated a Senate race would require the then-huge-for-Kansas sum of $1 million.
In the first quarter of 1978, she spent less than $12,000 on her campaign and saw herself “at the bottom of the totem pole.” However, nine candidates crowded the primary field, including three state senators and a prominent Wichita businessman. Kassebaum Baker won the GOP nomination with less than 31% of the vote.
Running as Nancy Landon Kassebaum, she won almost 54% of the vote that November against former two-term Democratic congressman Bill Roy.
Her moderate politics quickly came to the fore, when only months later, she refused to endorse an amendment to the U.S. Constitution to require a balanced budget.
“We should be wary of the seemingly simple solution,” she said.
Her father, who would die at age 100 in 1987, still cast a long political shadow during her first years in office. Though he'd overwhelmingly lost the 1936 presidential race to Democratic incumbent Franklin Roosevelt, he later became an elder statesman for the party. A lecture series named for him at Kansas State University attracted presidents and foreign leaders.
Kassebaum Baker became even more popular in her time. She won re-election in 1984 with 76% of the vote and in 1990 with 74% of the vote.
But she frustrated conservative activists, despite her popularity. She said her vote in favour of the assault weapons ban inspired the angriest mail of her career.
A public servant to the end
She'd contemplated not seeking a third term, but Republican leaders had prevailed upon her to run one more time. In 1996, when she decided not to seek re-election, she said she would return to a ranch and a 90-year-old farmhouse in Kansas' scenic Flint Hills and babysit her grandchildren — she had seven, as well as two great-grandchildren.
When there briefly was talk of naming a new highway in Topeka after her, she said, “Oh, goodness. Absolutely not — no.” She and Baker kept their romance low-key, and speculation about a possible marriage didn't emerge until mid-1996, in a Washington Post story. They married that December.
It was the first time a man and a woman who had both served in the Senate had wed. Baker was elected to three terms and served from 1967 to 1985 before becoming President Ronald Reagan's chief of staff. His first wife, Joy, had died in 1993 after a long battle with cancer.
After the marriage, public service still beckoned, including as a member of a bipartisan commission on campaign finance reform under Clinton and on a British commission in Africa in 2004-05.
President George W. Bush named her husband ambassador to Japan in 2001, and she went with him for the four-year posting. Baker said she became an important figure in the Asian nation.
Before she left for Tokyo, she told a reporter she saw her stint in Japan as an adventure but added, “All I can say is, I will miss the Kansas prairie.”
Not a fan of Trump
Later in life, Kassebaum Baker broke with the Republican Party as it became more conservative, endorsing Democratic candidates for Kansas governor and US senator, including Democratic Governor Laura Kelly both times — even though Kelly's 2022 GOP opponent, then state Attorney General Derek Schmidt, had worked on her Senate staff.
She also declared in 2021 that President Donald Trump should be impeached after Trump supporters attacked the US Capitol hoping to stop congressional certification of Trump's defeat in 2020 by Democrat Joe Biden.
“This just has gone too far,” she told Kansas City's KMBC.
