title: India vs Sri Lanka Tests: India holds egde as Sri Lanka looks to draw level
content:
From the incandescent natural beauty that Galle offered, Shubman Gill’s men have moved to the bustling metropolis that Colombo has always been. This multilingual city and a maritime junction, both for ancient and modern trade routes, was vital to Ceylon then and is equally critical to Sri Lanka now.
Also read | Visitors brave the heat in Colombo nets ahead of 2nd Test
Leading 1-0 and stepping into the second Test commencing at the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground in Colombo on Sunday (August 22, 2026), India holds the edge over Sri Lanka. The 165-run triumph at Galle will hold the visitors in good stead, a victory shaped by two young players — Devdutt Padikkal and Manav Suthar.
The pitch was a dull brown on match-eve, and fringed by the green outfield and rolled-up covers just in case it rained. Initial purchase for batters and later bonanzas for spinners, are the usual tropes associated with cricketing turfs in the Emerald Isle. And this surface will be no different.
In a batting unit that leant heavily on vice-captain K.L. Rahul and his Karnataka mate Padikkal, it is also time for Yashasvi Jaiswal and skipper Gill to join the party. Dhruv Jurel has done his bit in the middle-order and Rishabh Pant has been his robust self.
Even if Ravindra Jadeja offers batting solidity in the lower-order, India has a fragile tail, and it leaves the job of scoring runs entirely on the specialist batters. Countering the Sri Lankan spinners under shimmering heat that is intrinsic to the venue, will be a test of patience and technique.
Among the bowlers, Mohammed Siraj remains the spearhead with Prasidh Krishna having effected breakthroughs at Galle. While the spin-department is sorted with Suthar and Jadeja, there could be a swap between Kuldeep Yadav and Saransh Jain in the playing eleven. The latter’s off-spin could come in handy against left-handed batters.
For Sri Lanka, the fixture offers a chance to draw level in the series. Dinesh Chandimal, dealing with a concussion, will be missed in a batting order that is a touch short on experience. But the way Sonal Dinusha batted in the first Test, offered hope. At Galle, in the second innings, he was casually sitting on the side-wall, soaking in the sun, and awaiting his turn to bat.
Dinusha’s senior colleagues have to contribute as Sri Lanka needs big runs to exert scoreboard-pressure on India. A Test debut for Kamil Mishara is on the cards. The southpaw blitzed an unbeaten 145 in a recent domestic T20, but against India and in a Test, he would have to temper that innate aggression with caution.
The bulk of the home attack will lean on spinners Prabath Jayasuriya and Keshara Nuwantha. Their interrogation of the Indian batters would be the key that would determine how this game will proceed.
Gill’s men have ticked most of the boxes on this tour. They landed early, had a warm-up game, pocketed the Test at Galle, and in their last week in Sri Lanka, want to retain the feel-good factor. Sri Lanka, though, is keen on an ambush.

title: “Maybe at the Olympics, I’ll get a gold”: Praveen Chithravel on CWG, rehab
content:
Commonwealth Games silver medallist triple jumper Praveen Chithravel is confident of recovering from a blood clot in his right calf in time for the Aichi-Nagoya Asiad.
Chithravel has resumed training after a break. “I had been doing high-intensity training for five months. After the CWG, I was doing three weeks of load training for the Asian Games at the camp in the Czech Republic. The first week was good. I got a cramp while doing a take-off around August 10,” he told The Hindu on the sidelines of the World Athletics Continental Tour Silver meet at the Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar on Saturday (August 22, 2026).
“There is a blood clot. Initially, I couldn’t run. I took 10 days’ rest. I’ve started training from Monday — jogging and easy sessions. I’ve around a month for the Asian Games.”
The National record holder (17.37m in May 2023), who won bronze (16.68m) at the last Asiad despite a quadriceps issue, is not chasing a medal colour. “I want to do a good jump and end the season happily. If I jump 17.50m and finish fourth, I’ll be happy.”
Chithravel, who missed a medal by two centimetres to finish fourth (16.89m) in Birmingham 2022 — where Eldhose Paul and Abdulla Aboobacker won gold and silver — said his silver in Glasgow was four years in the making.
“I waited for this moment since 2022. I had a wallpaper on my phone. I knew a lot would change with this medal. So I worked hard, changed my technique and running approach and started training with Cuban coach Yoandri Betanzos.
“That day, I don’t know what happened to everyone. Medal-wise I’m happy, but performance-wise I’m not. Actually, it’s my gold. Maybe at the Olympics, I’ll get the gold.”
Chithravel has taken on a mentor’s role for Selva Prabhu, who won bronze in Glasgow. “Selva is the next generation, he is pushing me. Seniors supported me, so I’m supporting him. Arpinder Singh, Eldhose and Aboobacker, then it’s me and Selva. We want to keep the CWG medals. More triple-jumpers will come for 2030 CWG in India. I’m just 25, so I’ll be there for the next CWG and Asiad,” he said.

title: Paes applies to join AITA’s roster of SOM
content:
Indian tennis great and current Bengal Tennis Association (BTA) president Leander Paes has applied to join the All-India Tennis Association roster of Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM), BTA announced on social media on Friday.
According to the AITA’s amended constitution, a roster of 20 male and 20 female SOMs will be prepared, and out of that, two men and two women will be elected to the AITA General Body and will enjoy voting rights. Two SOMs – one man and one woman – will also be part of the 15-member Executive Committee.
SOMs elected to the General Body can apply to be in the EC, and can also contest for the posts of AITA president, general secretary and treasurer.
In fact, AITA started inviting applications from athletes to be part of the SOM roster on August 15, but wrote to the Union Sports Ministry on August 19 seeking to expand the selection criteria.
The National Sports Governance Act prioritises those with significant achievements in Olympics, Asian Games and Commonwealth Games, but the AITA has requested the addition of Grand Slams, ATP and WTA tournaments, and the Davis Cup and Billie Jean King Cup, all of which carry higher weightage in tennis.
Regardless, Paes will qualify as a Tier 1 SOM, courtesy his watershed singles bronze at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, which was India’s first individual medal at the quadrennial extravaganza after K.D. Jadhav’s in 1952.

title: Treesa and Gayatri rue defensive tactics and lack of patience
content:
On Friday, Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand had credited their victory to being calm on court and staying patient. On Saturday, the two admitted they had slipped up on both fronts in their three-game defeat to defending champions Sheng Shu Liu & Ning Tan in the semifinals of the badminton Worlds.
“I think today was just not our day. Towards the second half of the second game we lost our rhythm and they found theirs. They were constantly ahead of us and we just couldn’t catch up. When you play at this level, you need to be alert and in control on every point, points go by in the blink of an eye. They were also charging a lot on the net. A few mistakes were made and that also undermined our confidence. I think we were also a bit too defensive at one point,” a disappointed Treesa admitted after the match.
Gayatri agreed that the opponents relied on their experience and were a lot more patient. “They were more patient while we were lacking it today, just hurrying up and wanting points. They are World No. 1 and we knew they won’t give easy points. But it’s been an amazing week, we played some great matches, lots to learn from, including today’s loss,” she said.
Sheng and Ning, on their part, did admit that the opening game setback affected them but insisted that maintaining composure was important. “We are all nervous, especially in the first game when they overcame us. But I think we tried not to be affected in the second game, the match wasn’t over yet. We kept trying. In the third game, we just focused on our strengths and played at our own pace.”
The Chinese added that they weren’t wroiied about dropping a game for the first time in 10 matches. “I think it’s normal to fall behind, because the other team did a good job today, they are very strong opponents. We went prepared for it. But we overcame it. It’s also a lesson for the future, to keep in mind that you can lose the first game”.

title: East Bengal seeks redemption against Mohun Bagan as the traditional Kolkata rivals renew Durand Cup battle
content:
East Bengal FC will seek to avenge its only defeat of the season so far when its faces traditional rival Mohun Bagan Super Giant in the final of the 135th Durand Cup at Salt Lake Stadium on Sunday. The famed Kolkata Derby returns to the venue where this edition began four weeks ago, adding another layer to high-stakes contest.
The tournament opened with the derby which Mohun Bagan won 1-0 on July 25, with Sahal Abdul Samad scoring the decisive goal in the second half. Since then East Bengal has been flawless recording emphatic 8-0 and 5-0 group-stage victories before edging Indian Army 1-0 in the quarterfinal and overcoming Sporting Club Delhi via tie-breaker after a goalless semifinal.
Meanwhile, Mohun Bagan has remained unbeaten so far. After the derby triumph, Mohun Bagan dismantled South United FC 8-0 and CISF Protectors 6-0 before successfully navigating through the two tense knockout matches against Jamshedpur FC and NorthEast United FC on penalties.
The numbers suggest little to separate the finalists defensively - both have conceded just once in six matches. Mohun Bagan has 16 goals in favour to East Bengal’s 14, giving the Mariners a slight attacking edge. East Bengal has also shown the ability to negotiate tight knockout contests, which makes the final evenly balanced.
This will be the 13th Durand Cup final meeting between the rivals. They have won five finals each, while two others saw them ending as joint winners. Record 17-time champion Mohun Bagan can move to 18 titles with a victory, while East Bengal can draw level on 17.

title: Meghalaya launches mission to protect clouded leopards
content:
Meghalaya has launched a dedicated programme for its State animal—the mainland clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa).
On Tuesday (August 4, 2026), Chief Minister Conrad K. Sangma unveiled Mission Clouded Leopard. The feline is found in the State’s community-managed forests and in the forest landscapes of Nokrek, Balpakram, Baghmara, Narpuh and Nongkhyllem.
Also read: Understanding clouded leopards and their habitats
“The mission covers habitat protection and restoration, scientific research and long-term monitoring, stronger protection measures, landscape connectivity, capacity building of frontline staff, community participation, and public awareness. It will be guided by the Meghalaya Clouded Leopard Action Plan, now being prepared by the Forest and Environment Department,” the Chief Minister said.
“An ongoing scientific assessment has so far identified 21 individual clouded leopards in the Balpakram National Park. The assessment will be extended to all major habitats in the State, so that Meghalaya has, for the first time, a comprehensive population estimate of its State animal,” he said.
Distinct from the Sunda clouded leopard, which is found on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, the mainland clouded leopard is listed as “vulnerable” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, and protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
According to the Conservation Action Plan (CAP) for the caracal, fishing cat, and clouded leopard released by the Wildlife Institute of India on Tuesday, India supports one of the most important remaining populations of the mainland clouded leopard.
“Across its global range, important populations persist in Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, and parts of northeast India. In contrast, populations in Bangladesh, Vietnam, Taiwan, and large parts of China have undergone severe declines, with several regions now supporting only small and isolated populations or facing local extinction,” the CAP said.
The principal threats to clouded leopards include habitat loss, degradation, and fragmentation resulting from infrastructure development, agricultural expansion, mining, plantations, and human settlements. Illegal hunting and trade in skins and body parts continue to threaten populations across several range countries, while prey depletion, human disturbance, road development, and climate change further exacerbate conservation challenges.
“These threats are particularly significant because clouded leopards depend upon extensive, connected forest habitats and occur at naturally low population densities. The overall goal of the CAP is to secure viable, connected, and genetically healthy clouded leopard populations while conserving the forest ecosystems upon which they depend,” the action plan read.

title: Zubin Bharucha joins Mumbai Indians
content:
Zubin Bharucha has joined Mumbai Indians as its Director of Performance, switching franchises in a role that will see him work closely with the existing multi-disciplinary leadership group across performance disciplines.
“Zubin will join the current support staff within MI’s highly integrated ecosystem and build on Mumbai Indians’ established approach to delivering sustained excellence in player development,” a statement by MI read on Saturday.
The Hindu understands Bharucha will work alongside former Mumbai teammate Paras Mhambrey, an assistant coach with MI. The duo will be entrusted with the development pathway of Indian youngsters — both male and female — at the franchise’s training facility in Navi Mumbai on a year-long basis.
The appointment adds a former Mumbai opener whose coaching and player-development credentials have been built over more than a decade with Rajasthan Royals. Bharucha was instrumental in setting up and running year-long programmes at the Royals’ academy near Nagpur and played a key role in the development of several Indian youngsters, including Yashasvi Jaiswal, Dhruv Jurel, Riyan Parag and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.
Bharucha’s appointment is the first major change to Mumbai Indians’ support structure following an exhaustive review after the franchise’s disastrous IPL campaign. His mandate, however, extends beyond the immediate needs of the senior side, with the focus firmly on creating and strengthening the pathway for Indian talent within the MI ecosystem.
For MI, Bharucha’s experience in building a structured development programme offers an opportunity to strengthen an area that has increasingly become fragile for a set-up that was instrumental in creating scouting structure and grooming lesser-known talent.

title: Back to full fitness, Mayank savours the start of a new journey
content:
Pace is Mayank Yadav’s foremost ally. That was established in the blink of an eye in the 2024 Indian Premier League (IPL), where he went on to clock a top speed of 156.7 kmph for Lucknow Super Giants. With such a gift in his locker, he was predictably fast-tracked into the T20I set-up for a three-match series against Bangladesh in October that year.
While he equipped himself well to the challenge by picking four wickets at an economy rate of 6.91, a spate of injuries cast a shadow over the next 18 months. Most worryingly, a stress fracture in the back — a chink in the armour for most young speedsters — forced Mayank to undergo surgery and miss vast chunks of the cricketing calendar.
The upside is that the 24-year-old is now back to full fitness. On his comeback for India in a T20I series against Zimbabwe last month, he picked a wicket off his very first ball. He finished with five scalps in the series as the Men in Blue completed a clean sweep.
“To take a wicket off my first ball (against Zimbabwe) was a special feeling since I was returning after (almost) two years,” Mayank told the media on Friday. “It feels like my run of injuries is over. This is like the start of a new journey.”
In the ongoing Delhi Premier League, Mayank has built on his workload by featuring in six of East Delhi Riders’ eight games. He has claimed seven wickets at an average of 21.57.
“I’m feeling 100% fit. I came to play in the DPL after the Zimbabwe tour because I wanted a lot of game-time,” Mayank said.
During his time on the sidelines, the desire to wear the India jersey again helped the fast bowler retain a positive outlook.
“I played a lot of games on PlayStation when I was in rehab. It was a good pastime,” he revealed. “Mentally, to be in a good space, I was working towards the aim of representing the country again.”

title: Men’s hockey World Cup: Dutch enter semis; India on the brink of elimination
content:
India got a close up display on how to come up with a clinical performance at the hands of the Netherlands.
With six minutes to go, Manpreet Singh dawdled on the ball allowing Jorrit Croon to rob the ball and slip in Thijs van Dam. The forward flicked it over Mohith H.S., controlled it on the run, before slapping the ball into the net to finish off India in style..
In front of a packed Wagener Stadion, Netherlands sealed its place in the semifinal of the World Cup with a 3-1 win, pushing India to the brink of elimination here on Saturday. Argentina got the better of England 3-1 later in the day to boost its qualification chances.
Placed last, India needs to beat Argentina by a margin of four goals or more in its final Pool E match on Monday and hope that the Dutch defeat England on the same day.
Requiring a win, India put up a spirited fight, getting its tactics spot on to make the home side work hard, but familiar troubles in field play plagued Craig Fulton’s men. But the Dutch, picked apart India with three field goals, two of them coming from devastating counter-attacks.
Of the four matches in the tournament, this was India’s best start. Fulton’s side was sharper on the ball, controlling possession, not allowing the Dutch to play their flick passing game.
However, India, too, didn’t find space in the circle, struggling to find the right connections in field play. Dilpreet Singh came close but his deflected effort was booted away by Derk Meijer.
After trading blows again in the third quarter, the Dutch found momentum, before taking the lead. From a loose ball in the circle, Tijmen Rayenga’s shot-cum-pass was flicked in past Suraj Karkera by Duco Telgenkamp.
Chasing the equaliser, Harmanpreet Singh and Sanjay, unable to bypass the Netherlands press, were exchanging passes at the halfway line before the latter tried to force the initiative with a fizzed-in pass but went out of bounds.
Seconds later, the Netherlands turned defence into attack with three passes. Tjep Hoedemakers deflected the ball into the goal from a fierce Koen Bijen slapshot into the circle.
India responded immediately through Harmanpreet, finding the left bottom corner with his side’s sixth and final PC to halve the deficit.
But India’s hopes of a comeback were extinguished when Manpreet’s error was punished by van Dam.
The result: Netherlands 3 (Telgenkamp 40, Hoedemakers 50, van Dam 54) bt India 1 (Harmanpreet 51-pc).

title: Neeraj Chopra finishes second, Pathirage wins title in Lausanne Diamond League
content:
Indian javelin ace Neeraj Chopra produced his best performance in more than a year but was pipped to the post by the rising Sri Lankan star Rumesh Pathirage for the top spot by a mere nine centimetres in the Lausanne Diamond League meet in Lausanne on Friday (August 21, 2026).
The 28-year-old Chopra’s 88.05m throw in the second round, which fetched him the second spot in the nine-man star-studded field, was his best after the 88.16m he recorded while winning the Paris Diamond League in June 2025. It was also his season’s best throw.
However, the 23-year-old Pathirage continued his juggernaut this season as he overtook Chopra with his third-round throw of 88.14m.
Grenada’s Anderson Peters was third with his sixth and final round effort of 86.69m.
Reigning world champion Keshorn Walcott of Trinidad and Tobago was fourth with a best throw of 83.71m.
World Championships bronze winner Curtis Thompson of the USA was sixth with a below-par 78.13m, while Tokyo Olympics silver winner Jakub Vadlejch of the Czech Republic took the seventh spot with 77.32m.
Chopra later said it was a close tussle between him and Pathirage for the top spot.
“I didn’t realise it was only nine centimetres, it was really close, but I’m happy with the 88-metre throw. To be honest, it didn’t feel like it went 88m because I felt very relaxed. I tried really hard and later focused on my technique,” he said.
“With every competition, I feel that I’m coming back. The crowds in Lausanne and Zurich understand athletics and really support you, so it’s always good to compete here.” With his second-place finish, Chopra also jumped to top five in the season-ending Diamond League Finals standings from his earlier seventh spot.
For jumps and throws, the top six in the standings will compete in the September 4-5 DL Finals in Brussels. One additional athlete per discipline may also compete via a national or global wildcard selection.
Pathirage and Peters have already qualified for the DL Finals after accumulating 23 and 22 points, respectively. There is another DL meet which has a men's javelin throw event in it — in Zurich on August 27.
Chopra had won the DL Finals title in 2022 and finished second in 2023, 2024 and 2025.
The showdown between the two South Asian rivals lived up to the expectations, as Chopra sent his spear to 88.05m in his second attempt to overtake Pathirage and occupy the top spot briefly. The Sri Lanka responded soon after with his 88.14m effort in the third third to retake the spot.
This was the third time in a row that the 23-year-old Pathirage had beaten two-time Olympic medallist Chopra this year. He had earlier beaten the Indian superstar in the Doha Diamond League and then in the recent Glasgow Commonwealth Games. Pathirage had won in both the events, while Chopra had finished fourth and second, respectively.
Chopra began with 83.54m before coming up with a big throw of 88.05m. It was his season's best after his 85.83m while winning silver in the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. His third attempt measured 83.72m before recording a ‘No Mark’ in the fourth round.
Chopra then skipped the fifth round before coming up with 82.15m in his sixth and final attempt.
The reason for skipping the fifth throw could be that he wanted to keep himself safe and not exert much with the Asian Games coming up next month.
Crossing the 88m mark, however, would have given Chopra some confidence going ahead in the season after coming back from an injury. He responded to Pathirage’s throw of 87.06m to take the top spot after the second round, though the Sri Lankan came back in the third round to assert his supremacy.
The budding rivalry between the two South Asians was in full show after Pathirage clinched the gold and Chopra finished with a silver in the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.
Pathirage has been in the form of his life this season, having also won the Doha and Rome Diamond League meetings, besides clinching gold in Glasgow with a throw of 89.75m. He also breached the coveted 90m mark with a season-leading throw of 92.62m in Rome in June.
In fact, the Sri Lankan has won eight of the nine competitions he has participated in so far in the season.
Chopra, on the other hand, is on a comeback trail after recovering from a lower back injury that has troubled him since September last year.
The injury delayed his return until the Diamond League in Doha. He was not 100 per cent fit in Glasgow but was able to win a silver with a season’s best throw of 85.83m.
“I can’t say my fitness is there like before. But I’m getting there slowly,” Chopra had said at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.
One of the most consistent javelin throwers ever, two-time Olympic medallist Chopra has finished outside the top two in just two competitions in the last five years.
The Lausanne Diamond League was to see the most high-profile competition in recent memory but it has lost some shine with the pulling out of the reigning world champion Arshad Nadeem and newly-crowned European champion Julian Weber of Germany.

title: AUS vs BAN Day 1: Australia lose three wickets after skittling Bangladesh for 64
content:
Australia lost three quick wickets as Bangladesh fought back on day one of the second Test with the hosts 50-3 at tea after a Mitchell Starc masterclass skittled the visitors for just 64.
Skipper Pat Cummins won the toss in Mackay and his bowlers feasted on a fine day, determined to bounce back from a shock nine-wicket loss in the first Test at Darwin.
An irrepressible Starc was the destroyer in an incredible spell of swing and seam, taking five wickets in 22 balls during the morning session.
Bangladesh reached lunch at 35-6 and lasted barely an hour after the break as Starc and Cummins mopped up.
Only a last-wicket partnership of 25 between Taijul Islam (11 not out) and Shoriful Islam (14) took them past their lowest Test score of 43, against the West Indies in 2018.
Starc ended with 6-12 and Cummins took 3-25.
Australia started well in reply but then lost three wickets for 19 runs, leaving Steve Smith (six) and Cameron Green (one) with their work cut out.
Matt Renshaw, recalled for the first time since 2023 when opener Jake Weatherald was axed after Darwin, failed to repay selectors’ faith, gone for eight after edging Taskin Ahmed to Tanzid Hasan at third slip.
Fellow opener Travis Head (22) was bowled by Shoriful who missed the first Test with an injury, before he repeated the feat with under-pressure Marnus Labuschagne (4), who was desperate for a big score.
Australia made a stunning start when Starc removed Shadman Islam with the first ball of the day, tempting a leading edge that Green did well to hold in the gully.
It was the fourth time the veteran left-armer has got a wicket with the maiden ball of a Test -- becoming the first player to do so -- and the ninth time he has achieved the feat in the opening over.
The 36-year-old sent Bangladesh’s other opener Tanzid packing with the first ball of his second over, caught at slip by Beau Webster, then trapped captain Najmul Hossain Shanto lbw with his next delivery.
It left Bangladesh reeling at 3-9 in the third over.
The experienced Mushfiqur Rahim fended off Starc’s hat-trick ball, but he was unstoppable and grabbed his fourth wicket in his third over.
This time, Mominul Haque was the victim in a similar dismissal to Shadman, undone by late swing to send a thick edge low to Green in the gully on nine.
Webster dropped a sitter at slip off Starc in his fourth over, but Litton Das’ luck ran out next ball, out lbw on review as the visitors slumped to 5-12.
It was the 19th time Starc has taken five wickets in an innings and achieved in just 22 balls -- the sixth fastest of all-time.
Starc holds the record after taking five in only 15 balls against the West Indies in 2025.
Mushfiqur hung around for 41 balls but he had no answer when Cummins came on, bowled for five.
Cummins struck again after lunch to dismiss Mehidy Hasan Miraz for 11, taken brilliantly by Webster in the slips, before Hazlewood took care of Hasan Mahmud (10) eight balls later.
Bangladesh moved past their lowest Test score as the tailenders hit out, before Starc fittingly wrapped it up with the wicket of Shoriful.

title: Jockey Suraj Narredu makes India proud in Japan
content:
Jockey Suraj Narredu made India proud as he added yet another glorious chapter to his illustrious career by registering his first Japan Racing Association (JRA) victory at the Sapporo Racecourse in Japan on Saturday, August 22.
Adding to the pride of the occasion, the Japanese commentator referred to Suraj as “India’s Magic Man” while calling the race, a fitting tribute to the champion jockey’s remarkable talent and achievements.
In his first appearance on Japanese soil, Suraj partnered Fier Chanter trained by Kensuke Ogura, to victory in the 2,600m race for three-year-old maidens, producing a memorable triumph on the opening day of his historic stint in Japan.
Suraj had earlier finished fourth aboard Mont Royal in the third race (1,700m), his maiden event. He then celebrated his landmark JRA success when Fier Chanter scored in the sixth race.
In the two races of the 2026 World All-Star Jockeys Championship held on Saturday, Narredu’s results earned him a total of 10 points, placing him ninth in the standings after the opening day’s two legs.
The four-race championship brings together some of the finest riders from around the globe. The series is contested over different distances and surfaces, with points awarded according to finishing positions. Saturday’s first two legs were held over 1,200m and 2,000m on turf, while the remaining two races are scheduled for Sunday, August 23, over 1,700m on dirt and 1,800m on turf.
Narredu will have four rides at Sapporo on Sunday, partnering Trigonic, Cuthbert Tesoro, Itsumo Nikoniko and Bene Spira, with his final two rides coming in the concluding legs of the World All-Star Jockeys Championship.

title: India vs Sri Lanka Tests: Coach Gambhir says focus is on winning 2nd Test, not on WTC
content:
In his prime as an opener, Gautam Gambhir loved the scent of a battle and drew inspiration from it. The same combative streak lingers in his second avatar as the coach.
Speaking to the media at the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground here on Saturday (August 22), Gambhir was asked about criticism. The former India star was quick with his riposte: “I am here to win trophies!” Later, he added: “People in the press-box and commentators know that we are going through transition.”
Looking ahead to the second Test commencing on Sunday, Gambhir said: “Even if you score 1,000 runs, you still have to get 20 wickets; that’s how you win matches. So be it three left-arm spinners or an off-spinner or three seamers, we will take a call on what is the best team suited for this surface, it is about the team and the results.”
Praise for Padikkal, Suthar
Praising Devdutt Padikkal and Manav Suthar for their success in the first Test, Gambhir said: “It is encouraging to see them step up and perform straight away but then again we should not judge on just one or two performances. There will be ups and downs and we all know cricket is tough.”
The coach did not reveal if there would be a swap between Kuldeep Yadav and Saransh Jain, but he did tell about his chats with the former: “I want Kuldeep to just try and bowl good spells rather than looking desperate to take a wicket.”
Refusing to be drawn into a discussion over India’s chances in the ICC World Test Championship, Gambhir said the immediate focus is on the second Test. And as for players breaking down with injuries, he said: “We had a discussion; we want our best players to play as much cricket as possible.”
Three-Test series format ‘ideal’
Earlier, Gambhir backed the three-Test series format, terming it as ideal.
“A three-Test series gives a chance to a team that has lost the first Test to make a comeback and win the series.”
“You cannot do that in a two-Test series as the team that lost the first Test, at best, can only draw the series. Remember, it happened with India once after losing the first Test against Australia, the team could still make a comeback.”

title: Anusha Kutumbale eyes consistency in upcoming Table Tennis season
content:
For the better part of the last decade, Anusha Kutumbale’s father Shreesh has been the most animated spectator in the hall whenever his daughter takes to the table. There have been celebrations, disagreements, tantrums and, inevitably, hugs. Through the ups and downs of her career, though, he has remained the one constant. Be it as her coach, mentor, friend and obviously the father.
At 23, the Indore paddler is beginning to find a new kind of consistency herself. Anusha enters the new domestic season at the UTT National Ranking Table Tennis tournament in Kanpur with confidence fuelled by a year that has offered both validation and frustration. She played a key role in U Mumba TT’s successful Ultimate Table Tennis title defence in July, while her run to the WTT Feeder final in Vadodara in January provided another reminder of her ability to challenge the established order.
It was in Vadodara, in August 2025, that she had won the opening National Ranking tournament of the previous season. But what followed was a topsy-turvy campaign, culminating in a seventh-place finish in the national rankings and a narrow miss for India’s Asian Games squad.
Rather than dwell on the disappointment, Anusha chose to work on herself — quite literally. “I have stopped thinking about what my professional career trajectory should be,” she says. “Instead of thinking ahead about what lies ahead, I am just going to leave the planning to somebody else. I am just going to go out there and do what I do.”
That “somebody else” is, unsurprisingly, her father.
The transformation in Anusha over the past year has been evident. She has become leaner and fitter, while working on retaining muscle and strengthening her core. She insists the objective was never to lose weight.
“Very honestly, the goal was never to lose weight. It was always to become fitter, stronger,” she says.
A major part of that process came after she joined Athletes Aura, a performance centre in Indore. The environment, she says, helped make fitness less of an obligation and more of a habit.
“When everyone uplifted each other, I started to actually want to become fitter, want to become stronger. And it became part of the routine,” she says. “Personally also, it helped me a lot with how I see myself, be it with self-image or with discipline.”
The first tangible evidence came in Vadodara national ranking. Anusha had four matches in a day, each of them demanding. In the past, she had often found that stretching herself over a long day came with a price the following morning. This time, she woke up ready for another test — a semifinal against Diya Chitale.
“That was the time when I knew that the work I had put in for my fitness had paid me,” she says.
Her ability to withstand the physical demands of a long tournament was more than a fitness marker. It offered Anusha the confidence that her body could now support the ambitions of her game.
That confidence was evident in UTT, where she contributed to U Mumba’s title defence. And when the pressure of the fifth match arrived, she found herself embracing rather than fearing it.
“My coaches (John Murphy and Jay Modak) and my team prepped me really, really well,” she says. “Right from day one, they’ve been telling me to just go out there, play my game and enjoy the feeling of being in a situation where I do get a lot of attention. I see it as attention and not as pressure and just try to enjoy myself.”
It is a mindset that has perhaps been shaped by the disappointments of the previous season. After winning in Vadodara and reaching the Feeder final, Anusha eventually found herself seventh in the national rankings and outside India’s Asian Games squad. Instead of allowing the uncertainty over her career path to consume her, she has consciously chosen to narrow her focus.
The next point. The next match. The next tournament.
In the background, the voice of the man who has been there since she first picked up a racket. “He is like the backbone. Without him, I cannot stand,” Anusha says of her father. “In the back of my mind, I am having conversations with him when I am playing, even when he is not there.”
Their journey, however, has not been without friction. A father coaching his daughter inevitably brings emotional moments, and Anusha admits there have been plenty of fights and tantrums.
“But I trust him more than anything in the world,” she says. “Whenever I am in a clutch moment, I remember him and all the strength comes to me.” The trick, they have learnt over time, is not to let what happens at the table spill over into their relationship away from it.
“We have really worked consciously towards that,” she says. “No matter what happens on the table, even if you have the worst fights and he has to deal with a lot of my tantrums, end of the day, I still go and sit in his lap and hug him and everything is OK.”
For now, Anusha’s attention returns to the table. The opening National Ranking tournament of the new season offers a familiar setting and an opportunity for an encore.
Vadodara gave her the breakthrough last season. Kanpur could provide another marker in a topsy-turvy career that is increasingly beginning to look deliberate.

title: Women’s Hockey World Cup: India goes down fighting to Netherlands, suffers first loss
content:
There was an orange wave sweeping the stands as the Wagener Stadion was bathed in the summer sunlight, well past the Friday (August 21, 2026) evening pushback.
Yibbi Jansen, the Netherlands’ lethal drag-flicker, scored her seventh goal of the World Cup to put the host 1-0 up after just 83 seconds. The home supporters were anticipating a blue wave on the turf with India’s new colours forcing the Dutch to switch to their away uniform. But India resisted in a hard-fought 2-0 loss in the second round of the tournament.
The win sent the three-time defending champion into the semifinals while India sits fourth in the standings. But the 1-1 draw between Australia and China, earlier in the day, left the door still open for India to challenge for a spot in the semifinals.
After being pushed to the limit just over 24 hours ago, the Indian team struggled to get out of its own half as passes went astray or solo runs ended in cul-de-sacs against the Dutch’s full-court press. India withstood two more penalty corners from the stick of Jansen with Bichu Devi making a block before another drag-push struck the post.
India grew in confidence with neat passing moves, but Salima Tete blazed over, and Navneet Kaur flashed wide. Deepika had two PCs but were shut out by the Netherlands’ defence.
After the break, India had a glorious chance to go level from a counter-attack but Sunelita Toppo’s tame effort was saved by Anne Veenendaal. Against the world’s best, goal-scoring chances are hard to come by and soon after, the Netherlands let it know. Frederique Matla beat Ishika Chaudhary on the line with a drag-flick to double the advantage.
Exhaustion finally caught up with Sjoerd Marijne’s women as they struggled to hold on to possession with unforced errors. Freeke Moes threatened to widen the margin when she forced Savita Punia into a save from close range before her rebound came off the post.
The mood at the final hooter wasn’t one of despair for the Indian women after suffering their first loss of the campaign as they will know this isn’t the end.
The result:
Netherlands 2 (Jansen 2-pc, Matla 37-pc) bt India 0.

title: Christos Tzolis shines as Arsenal start title defence with a bang
content:
Newcomer Christos Tzolis helped set up two goals as defending champion Arsenal opened the Premier League season by dismantling promoted Coventry 3-0 to spoil the visitor's long-awaited return to the top flight Friday (August 21, 2026).
After ending a 22-year wait for the Premier League title, Arsenal showed why it's favoured to repeat as champion by completely dominating Frank Lampard's side in a game that was one-sided from start to finish.
Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and captain Martin Odegaard scored for the Gunners, who spurned chances to pad the scoreline even further.
“The perfect start,” Odegaard said.
For Coventry, it was a rude welcome back to the Premier League after a 25-year absence. Having won the second-tier Championship last season by a wide margin, Lampard's side simply looked outmatched as it was repeatedly taken apart by a marauding Arsenal.
Tzolis was the only summer signing to start for the host but the left winger showed he could give this attack an added dimension by helping to set up both opening goals.
First he stole possession to feed defender Riccardo Calafiori, who squared the ball for Havertz to slot home in the 15th minute. The Greece international then sent a cross in from the left that goalkeeper Carl Rushworth managed to only push into the path of Saka, who scored into an empty net in the 23rd.
"Amazing, he played a brilliant game," Odegaard said of Tzolis. "He has been brilliant all preseason. He's so lively, it's hard to defend him. He's a really intelligent player, he always looks up and finds the right pass.”
Odegaard added the third shortly after the break after his scuffed shot looped in out of reach of Rushworth. The Arsenal captain gave an apologetic shrug as a celebration.
"It was not the best finish but I was there,” Odegaard said.
At the other end, the only time Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya was troubled was when a speculative overhead kick from Loum Tchaouna from outside the box sailed just high of the bar in the 42nd. The visitor's only effort on target came in the 86th, when Jack Rudoni managed only a weak header straight at Raya.
Arsenal introduced its latest signing, England defender Ezri Konsa, before kickoff after he completed a move from Aston Villa earlier Friday.

title: FIFA slaps Argentina with fines, bans over World Cup final
content:
A 10-match suspension for midfielder Leandro Paredes was one of several sanctions FIFA imposed against Argentina on Friday (August 22, 2026) for their actions in last month’s World Cup final loss to Spain.
The FIFA Disciplinary Committee also fined Paredes $90,000 for sparking a post-match brawl after Spain’s 1-0 victory in extra time on July 19 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J.
Argentina teammates Nahuel Molina (seven-match suspension, $90,000 fine) and Thiago Almada (one match, $30,000) and team official Roberto Ayala (three matches, $30,000) and Spain midfielder Gavi (one match, $30,000) also were disciplined.
FIFA also fined the Argentinian Football Association (AFA) $321,000 for various violations, including using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature; team misconduct; and discriminatory chants and gestures by its supporters. Argentina was ordered to invest $100,000 of their fine in a plan to combat discrimination.
Argentina must also play their next two home matches with a spectator capacity limit of 50%, although one of the two matches and $100,000 of the fine are suspended during a probationary period.
Paredes, 32, who plays professionally with Argentina’s Boca Juniors, received a red card after the loss to Spain when he charged Spain defender Eric Garcia, grabbed him by the throat and knocked him to the turf. Video from the post- match scrum appeared to show Molina and Ayala throwing punches at opposing players.
The “demonstrations of a non-sporting nature” occurred when several Argentina players unfurled a banner about the Falkland Islands after their semifinal win against England. The banner read, “The Falklands are Argentine” and referenced the United Kingdom’s 1982 war with Argentina over possession of the islands.

title: Sreeja’s qualification placement raises eyebrows
content:
Minutes before the Under-17 boys’ and girls’ finals at the UTT National Ranking Table Tennis tournament at The Sportz Hub on Friday (August 21, 2026), Sreeja Akula was completing her final qualification-round match.
The India women’s captain for the Asian Games, ranked No. 57 in the world, made short work of Shivasri S. to enter the main draw before returning to the gallery to support fellow coach Somnath Ghosh’s protégé Vivaan Dave in the Under-17 boys’ final.
While Sreeja had no qualms about starting from the qualifiers, the sight of India’s highest-ranked women’s paddler doing so did not sit well with some veterans.
“It is ridiculous to see India’s top player being made to play the qualifiers,” said former international Sunil Babras, now a coach with the Petroleum Sports Promotion Board.
Competition manager N. Ganesan, however, said the technical team was “merely following the tournament prospectus”.
The prospectus, based on a TTFI AGM decision in July 2024, stipulates that players ranked in the “ITTF top 50 at the time of the first draw” receive the top seeding, with the remaining seeding determined by the “latest national rankings”. The top 16 players in the domestic rankings are then seeded accordingly.
Sreeja’s domestic ranking slipped to No. 27 after injuries and international commitments restricted her participation only to the Senior Nationals during the previous season.
This is not the first such instance. A. Sharath Kamal also began the 2021 edition from the qualifiers before going on to win the title.
Dave and Bhowmick clinch titles
Eighth seed Vivaan Dave ended his dream run in boys’ under-17 in style, while Divyanshi Bhowmick justified her top billing by claiming the singles titles.

title: Abnormal service resumes: the 2026 F1 season rolls on
content:
The 2026 season of Formula One ushered in some of the most drastic regulatory changes in the sport’s history. As teams and drivers still try to get around the new cars, the year’s first half has been a mixed bag for on-track action. Nonetheless, there has been enough to keep the fans interested. With the F1 carnival reconvening after the summer break in Zandvoort this weekend, The Hindu reviews the major themes so far to see what could lie ahead.
Energy-starved cars
The new rules, which brought hybrid power units closer to a 50-50 split between the internal combustion engine and the electric motor, raised concerns at the outset that the cars would be energy-starved. When pre-season testing began, four-time champion Max Verstappen was scathing in his criticism. The battery’s limitations meant drivers had to ease off through fast corners to maximise electric power on straights, where time could be gained.
Add to it the complex algorithms governing how the battery deploys and harvests energy, and drivers were forced to adapt their driving styles to the car’s limitations. In the first few races, this led to cars being passed and then passing back as the battery pack emptied and recharged, resulting in ‘yo-yo racing’. The fans were none the wiser, as one couldn’t ascertain whether the moves were genuine. It took time for teams to adapt, and a rule tweak in Miami has also helped reduce some of the worst effects of ‘yo-yo racing’. Still, on energy-hungry tracks, the sight of F1 cars unwilling to be driven in anger around fast corners has dampened the spectacle.
Breakout star
One of the great joys of watching elite sport is to marvel at the ability of a wonderkid ruffling the feathers of the established order. Even as F1 has been besieged by negativity around the new regulations, the one bright light has been Kimi Antonelli. The Italian, who will graduate out of his teens on Tuesday (August 25), has taken the F1 world by storm in his sophomore campaign, winning six of the 11 races and leading the championship by 50 points.
The Mercedes driver has taken a clear step up from his error-strewn rookie year, stringing together five consecutive wins at one stage. His aggressive driving style, with sharp steering inputs, seems to work well with the current cars, and the youngster has made full use of the class-leading Mercedes to build a comfortable lead. Team boss Toto Wolff’s decision to throw him in the deep end last year appears a stroke of genius.
While Antonelli has a healthy lead, he has already experienced how fickle it can be. He was once 66 points ahead and saw that whittled down to 25 before he built it back up. With a possible 12 races left this year, it is too early to pop the champagne. However, if he keeps doing what he has been doing, keeping a calm head, he could etch his name into the history books.
Plight of the presumptive favourite
George Russell bided his time in an uncompetitive Williams for three years before earning a promotion to Mercedes in 2022 to partner Lewis Hamilton. Unfortunately, it came at a time when the German marque, which had won eight successive titles, messed up the 2022 ground-effect regulations. He was saddled with a car that could at best fight for the occasional win. But in his three years alongside Hamilton, Russell showed he could go toe-to-toe with one of the greatest drivers in history. By the end of 2024, he was faster.
So when he won the first race in Australia from pole and then dominated the sprint in China, he would have felt that his patience was finally paying off. Yet, it has pretty much been downhill since then. A mixture of reliability issues, bad luck during races, and his driving style not suiting the current car has left the presumptive pre-season favourite 59 points off top spot.
We will soon know whether Russell has found a way during the summer break to address the pace deficit to his colleague. The title fight could still be between the Mercedes drivers; they have the best package. But the last few races have shown that Ferrari and McLaren are not far off. It is an extra set of variables that the 28-year-old could have done without.
Hamilton’s revival
Even as Russell has endured a torrid time, his former teammate has found a new lease of life after four years of struggle in ground-effect cars. Hamilton’s initiation into Ferrari was tumultuous, and there were times last year when one wondered if the seven-time champion was past his best. In fact, the Briton himself pondered if he was the right man for the job. However, the nimble 2026 cars seem to have rekindled his mojo and the 41-year-old is now second in the standings.
His hard work at the factory has helped him build a better relationship with the team, which was far from smooth last year. More importantly, the team has also given in to some of his demands, especially regarding the brakes, allowing him to use his preferred Carbone Industrie discs even though Ferrari has a long-standing relationship with rival Brembo. Hamilton’s better feel for the brakes has allowed him to exploit the car better, and the result was his first win for Ferrari in Barcelona.
While the title challenge is still a long shot, Hamilton will feel that if he can get good results in the next few rounds, the pursuit of that elusive eighth crown will start to become more real.
Max’s Red Bull situation
Verstappen and Red Bull have long maintained that the new-era cars aren’t fun to drive. They have also spoken extensively about the limitations of the power unit. While some called it fearmongering, given that Red Bull was building its own engines for the first time, reality has, to an extent, caught up with what they were warning about.
Although Red Bull has done a tremendous job on the powertrains, its electric component is not as strong as Mercedes’. Combine that with a lack of aerodynamic stability and a faulty rear wing, and it’s no surprise that Verstappen is far from happy with his team. This led to rumours that the Dutchman was trying to leave Red Bull or even walk away from the sport.
But, on the eve of this weekend’s Dutch GP, Verstappen extended his contract up to 2030, showing a commitment to the project under Laurent Mekies, who took over from Christian Horner last year. The Red Bull boss has done a good job of ensuring the team’s biggest asset stays. However, there is now added pressure on him and the engineers to repay Verstappen’s faith and provide him a car worthy of his generational talent.

title: Kerala Cricket League | Vinil, Azharuddeen fashion Ripples’ facile win
content:
Left-arm pacer T.S. Vinil’s fiery spell upfront and Mohammed Azharuddeen’s blitzkrieg during the chase powered Alleppey Ripples to an eight-wicket win over Trivandrum Royals in the Kerala Cricket League at the Sports Hub Greenfield Stadium on Friday.
Vinil’s spell in the PowerPlay, which included a double wicket maiden over, broke the back of Royals batting and it limped to 126 for eight in 20 overs. Azharuddeen (68, 29b, 8x4, 5x6), who was dropped on eight by Sijomon Joseph, sewed up the contest in the PowerPlay. After Azharuddeen’s dismissal, skipper Sachin Baby (26 not out) and K.A. Arun (24 not out) guided Ripples home with 43 balls to spare.
There was no hint of a Royals collapse when Vishnu Vinod smoked the first ball of the match from Vinil through covers for a boundary. However, Vinil’s twin strikes in the second over changed the contest on its head. Vinil got the ball to jag back and pinned Vishnu (7) in front and dismissed Abhishek P. Nair for a duck.
When Royals’ skipper Krishna Prasad was run out, trying to go for a non-existent third, the team slumped to 26 for four in the PowerPlay. Sijomon (46) and K. Ajeesh (23) counterattacked to add 39 runs for the seventh wicket which enabled Royals to cross 100.
Azharuddeen started imperiously, spanking Vinod Kumar for consecutive boundaries, but Sijomon, at covers, failed to latch on a mistimed drive from the batter in the same over. Azhar made Royals pay for the grave error and took the game away with his scintillating knock.
Narrow victory
In the second match of the day, Calicut Globstars scored a thrilling three-run win to snap holder Kochi Blue Tigers’ eight-match unbeaten run across two seasons. Chasing 149 for a win, Tigers was dismissed for 145 in the 19th over.
Earlier, Globstars recovered from 43 for four in the eighth over to post 148 for five, thanks to Salman Nizar (47 not out, 37b, 2x4, 2x6) and Krishna Devan (40 not out, 17b, 2x4, 4x6) clubbing 54 runs off 27 balls for the sixth wicket.
The scores: Trivandrum Royals 126/8 in 20 overs (Sijomon Joseph 46, T.S. Vinil 3/19, Jalaj Saxena 2/22) lost to Alleppey Ripples 127/2 in 12.5 over (Mohammed Azharuddeen 68, Sachin Baby 26 n.o.).

title: GCL chairperson expects Bengaluru edition to be well received
content:
The Global Chess League, the fourth edition of which opens at Bengaluru on September 5, is aiming to bring the mind sport closer to the common man even as it is attracting new investors, including a football World Cup winner.
The GCL chairperson Peeyush Dubey is delighted that former Spanish defender Gerard Pique has picked up a stake in the franchise Fyers American Gambits, whose owners include former India cricketer R. Ashwin.
“The fact that Piquet has become an investor shows the global interest the GCL has generated,” Dubey told The Hindu over the phone from New Jersey. “Most of the sponsors associated with the league in Mumbai last year are with us for this season too, and there are some new entrants as well.”
This is for the second year in a row that the GCL, a joint venture between Tech Mahindra and global chess governing body FIDE, is being held in India, after the first two editions were staged in Dubai and London. “Our team owners, who are predominantly companies based out of India, always wanted us to be in India” he said. “This is where their customers and audience are; and they are able to attract them, and we saw that happening in Mumbai.”
Dubey is confident that Bengaluru would also respond to the GCL with as much enthusiasm. “Bengaluru has been a city that we were very keen in exploring in terms of how it has been talking about the game, how the technology as a technology company that Tech Mahindra is, how Bengaluru offers that kind of alignment as well with how we are looking at chess,” he said. “And, of course, we work with all our franchises and the larger ecosystem to select the city.”
He expects the Bengaluru edition to be bigger than the Mumbai one. “I think last year’s league was very well received across all over the country and all over the world,” he said. “We reached more than 211 million people across the media. For Season-4, we have already received a lot of interest from various institutions, be it schools or chess clubs in Bengaluru.”

title: My confidence has increased after the CWG bronze, says Yashvir Singh
content:
With renewed confidence, Commonwealth Games bronze medallist Yashvir Singh is trying to improve a few areas of his game to emerge as a better javelin thrower.
Yashvir, who would compete in the World Athletics Continental Tour Silver meet at the Kalinga Stadium here on Saturday, said he had been fine-tuning his throws under his father-cum-coach Rai Singh.
“I am working under my father’s guidance on technical faults, speed and blocking lag. My father had a dream which he couldn’t achieve. He threw around 75m and competed at the National level. Now he is working as a Railways coach,” said Yashvir.
“All the time we discuss javelin,” said Yashvir, sharing that Rai is not too strict as a coach as the father-son duo don’t mind having ice-cream together.
Yashvir, who achieved 85.41m in his last throw in the CWG, said his confidence increased after sharing the podium with Worlds and Olympic medallist Neeraj Chopra, who took the silver in Glasgow.
“The competition was good. I got my best performance and a medal. This is the first time that we won two medals. After that, my confidence is really good. I have competed with such big athletes and gained experience.”
On his target from the Silver meet, Yashvir said, “I will try to give a better performance. Last year, I participated in the Bronze Level competition and finished sixth. I will try to give my 100 per cent.
“There are international athletes from Sri Lanka and South Africa who have participated in the CWG. The competition will be good and we will get more motivation from it,” said Yashvir.

title: Who will seize control of the post-Pep Premier League era?
content:
The 10 years Pep Guardiola spent at Manchester City represent one of the greatest acts of dynasty-building in the sporting universe.
Not only did the Catalan coach City to six Premier League titles, five League Cups, three FA Cups, one UEFA Champions League crown and one at the FIFA Club World Cup, he did so by assembling multiple great sides, revolutionising tactics, and constantly reinventing himself.
Dominant reign
Guardiola’s six Premier League trophies are second only to Alex Ferguson’s 13 at Manchester United, and even in the four years when City did not win the top prize, it stayed in the top three. No other coach won more than one Premier League title during Guardiola’s time in England.
When such a king abdicates the throne and leaves his kingdom, as Guardiola did at the end of the 2025-26 campaign, there is bound to be an almighty jostle among those below to be the immediate heir. The 2026-27 Premier League season, which got underway late on Friday (August 21), will be the battleground to decide whom the power is transferred to.
The setting is conducive for an intriguing competition. City without Guardiola will be one of nine clubs to have new coaches, and two others in Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur did not have Michael Carrick and Roberto De Zerbi in place at the start of the year.
Mikel Arteta, who secured Arsenal its first English top-flight crown in 22 years, is the most experienced, having been in the job for a little over six years and seven months. Unai Emery, who masterminded Aston Villa’s 2025-26 Europa League triumph, is next, with a stint now at roughly three years and 10 months.
Though Guardiola has exited the scene, his giant shadow still looms. Enzo Maresca, who has replaced the 55-year-old at the Etihad, and Arteta have served as his assistants. Xabi Alonso, installed as Chelsea’s new manager, was once Guardiola’s midfield marshal at Bayern Munich.
The post-Pep Premier League era will not have a clean break in terms of tactics too, for Guardiola has left a deep imprint, both in terms of the first principles he introduced, and how he evolved and shed his orthodoxies to cater to the League’s fast-changing demands.
When he first arrived, Guardiola was a cleric of the possession-heavy school and was canonical in his belief that retaining the ball was the best route to success. So much so that even goalkeepers weren’t spared; one of his first decisions at City was to replace Joe Hart, a top-class shot-stopper, with Claudio Bravo, a ball-playing goalie.
And it felt like the league as a whole — with the glorious exception of Jose Mourinho’s Manchester United — was trying to inculcate parts of it.
Guardiola then changed tack to embrace high-energy players and those with great individual skills in order to adjust to the breathless, end-to-end football that the likes of Jurgen Klopp (Liverpool) and Mauricio Pochettino (Tottenham) introduced. The controlled aggression of the earlier years made way for a more expressive and expansive style.
Philosophical blasphemy
And in his last four seasons in charge, he played with one of world football’s purest strikers in Erling Haaland. For a man who once made Lionel Messi turn out as a False 9, and then won two Premier League trophies in 2020-21 and 2021-22 with midfielders as top-scorers (Ilkay Gundogan with 13 goals and Kevin de Bruyne 15), to have Haaland score 112 times over four campaigns would have been akin to philosophical blasphemy.
However, football is now more direct and physical than in recent times and it is to Guardiola’s credit that he tweaked his methods and put in place a blueprint for success. “You need to adapt, evolve,” City’s Maresca said recently. “Set-pieces, man to man — it’s a little bit the direction where football is going. We managers… it’s our duty to find solutions.”
Who among Arteta, Carrick, Alonso, Andoni Iraola and Maresca will answer the call? For one, the sight of Arteta, Carrick and Alonso walking briskly up and down the touchline is sure to remind fans of their glory days as players for Arsenal, Manchester United and Liverpool not so long ago. For a certain generation, it will appear like they are reliving a childhood dream.
Arteta has the first-mover advantage, having already won the League and possessing a winning combination. The addition of Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle for GBP 75 million will reduce the inordinate burden on midfielder Declan Rice. But Arsenal’s unsuccessful pursuit of Vinicius Junior suggests that the outfit is mindful of the need of a world-class threat upfront.
Carrick, who took over at Old Trafford after the sacking of Ruben Amorim, had an impressive stint as caretaker manager, winning 12 and drawing three of his 17 matches in 2025-26, and helping United qualify for the Champions League after a two-season hiatus. The question before the astute 45-year-old is whether his United has the quality to sustain simultaneous domestic and continental challenges.
For Alonso, Chelsea is the opportunity to light up an aura that has seemingly dimmed after a failed seven-month stint as Real Madrid’s boss. The 44-year-old is known to possess a shrewd tactical brain, and his role in ending Bayern Munich’s hegemony in Germany — 11 straight Bundesliga titles from 2012-13 to 2022-23 — by leading a young Bayer Leverkusen side to its maiden crown is noteworthy. The addition of 24-year-old English attacking midfielder Morgan Rogers for a whopping GBP 117 million shows that he has Chelsea’s wholehearted trust.
Andoni Iraola’s ascent to the top job at Liverpool after making a mark at Bournemouth is eerily similar to Graham Potter’s entry into Chelsea in 2022 after a stellar show at Brighton & Hove Albion. But Potter was dismissed in less than seven months, a fate Iraola will want to avoid.
The 44-year-old is agnostic to any style of play that is not front-footed, a factor that endeared him to the Liverpool hierarchy after a dreary end to Arne Slot’s time. Can he manage to keep the club faithful happy without the services of Mohamed Salah, who left after nine glorious years?
Tough act to follow
Maresca’s situation at City is comparable to what David Moyes faced at United after the latter succeeded Ferguson in 2013. The Italian’s first test will be to not get crushed under the burden of expectations after Guardiola’s supremely successful tenure. It helps that City is not known to be trigger-happy, for both Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini enjoyed tenures lasting three years or more before Guardiola arrived.
Maresca also comes with a certain pedigree, having led Chelsea to FIFA Club World Cup glory in 2025, and has added England midfielder Elliot Anderson for a hefty GBP 116 million fee. But he will have to compete without the talismanic World Cup winner Rodri, who has shifted to Barcelona, and fellow playmaker Bernardo Silva, who has moved to Real Madrid.
Will he be guided by the spirit of Guardiola or will the ghost of Guardiola haunt him?

title: Badminton World Championships | We are not stopping here, say Treesa and Gayatri
content:
‘Keep calm and carry on,’ Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand kept telling each other en route to a historic quarterfinal win against Jia Yifan and Shuxian Zhang, a pair that has between them five medals at the World Championships and two at the Olympics.
It was forgotten the moment Yifan sent the shuttle wide on match point, Gayatri sprawling on the court and Treesa rushing to hug Pullela Gopichand and B. Sumeeth Reddy in the coaches’ corner.
They broke down, took a long break before returning to answer questions and for once, no one grudged the Indian youngsters.
“It was really difficult with all the emotions and processing what had finally happened but we are ok now,” Treesa admitted. “We are really happy to get into the semifinals and confirm a medal but we are not stopping here. There are matches still to come,” she declared, making it clear that the pair was not yet done.
Next up would be the top-seeded pair of Sheng Shu Liu & Ning Tan but when asked about the match, Gayatri insisted there would be little change in the mindset.
“We don’t want to think too much about the outcome. Today was also a tough match, we knew it would not be easy. We were trailing by a game and even in the second, it was tricky. We told each other to stay calm and will do the same tomorrow, get on court and give our 100 percent and just enjoy,” she added.
Gayatri has made no secret of Gopichand the father’s strict regimen, but on Friday there were no complaints about Gopichand the coach from either.
“When we started as partners, he was the one who told us he believed we could achieve something big. It is really special to have him in the chair, he has been a big support and I am grateful he can travel with us.
“He was telling us to just stay calm, stay in the present and that really helped. There have been a few tournaments where I have messed up with my greediness to score quickly. Today we were not greedy, we were just being patient and waiting for the right moments to the points.”

title: TNPL: Shahrukh Khan powers Kovai Kings to crucial win
content:
M. Shahrukh Khan wasn’t at his best in the first six matches of TNPL-10, but it seemed the Vida Kovai Kings skipper was saving his best for the last.
In a must-win final league game for his side, the swashbuckling batter unfurled his full repertoire of bludgeoning strokes, smashing an unbeaten 18-ball 59 (4x4, 6x6), to set up Kovai Kings’ thumping 85-run victory (DLS method) over Dindigul Dragons here at the MAC Stadium on Friday.
Put in to bat, Kovai Kings openers S. Radhakrishnan and S. Lokeshwar got the team off strongly, collecting 56 in the PowerPlay. With Kings at 96 for three in 12.1 overs, a heavy downpour stopped proceedings for 75 minutes.
Once the game resumed - truncated to 16 overs per side - Shahrukh wasted no time in raining sixes as the two-time champion plundered 75 runs in the remaining 3.5 overs to amass 171 for three.
The 31-year-old pulled leggie Nirankar Sharma over midwicket for his first maximum, and it was a sign of things to come. In the next over, he went after Sandeep Warrier, tonking him for three boundaries and a six in a 23-run over.
Shahrukh then closed it out in style with a hat-trick of sixes off pacer S. Karuppasamy, the second of which took him past his half-century.
Chasing a revised target of 179, Dragons hit trouble straightaway, losing opener Shivam Singh off the first delivery. From there it was all downhill for the 2024 champion. Left-arm spinner M. Siddharth scalped two wickets in the fourth over, and later Jhathavedh Subramanyan struck thrice in the eighth over to reduce Dragons to 59 for six and seal the contest in Kovai’s favour.
Later in the evening, Trichy Grand Cholas became the first team to qualify for the Playoffs, beating Chepauk Super Gillies by 14 runs and moving to the top of the table with 10 points. Opting to bat, Grand Cholas made 191 for seven, riding on half-centuries from S. Shyam Sundar and Sanjay Yadav.

title: Hockey World Cup | Time to buckle up for tougher games, says India men’s coach Craig Fulton
content:
India head coach Craig Fulton has called for his men to refocus ahead of what he calls a ‘new tournament’ in the second round of the men’s World Cup, starting against Netherlands on Saturday.
India’s mixed start in the Pool stage led to a second place finish behind England, which has left it needing two wins to give itself a good chance of qualifying for the semifinals.
“We’re a little bit behind the eight ball because we didn’t take the three points through. But at this level as well, any team can beat any team,” Fulton told The Hindu.
“That doesn’t mean we’re out. We have to take care of our two games. We’ll just go one game at a time and let’s see what happens.”
A deficient defensive structure and unforced errors leaving it open to transitions have proved costly. India has let in eight goals, which is the worst defensive record among the top eight teams left in the tournament.
Fulton emphasised on getting the pressing right and its counterattacks with upcoming matches against two of the dangerous sides, Netherlands and Argentina.
India’s recent meetings against these sides yielded just one 3-2 win over the Dutch, while losing the other three with an aggregate scoreline of 4-15.
“It’s a game [vs Pakistan] that is steeped in history, where we need to take more structure into that game, and it got away from us a little bit.
“But at the same time, we played well offensively and then let them back in the game...Now, we have a totally different opposition, that if we give them too many opportunities, yes, they will punish you.
“We’re playing well going forward, and we need to keep improving on the defence and keeping the confidence in going forward. So the press, the counter, is where we need to just keep hammering,” said the South African.
While Harmanpreet Singh’s form makes India a lethal Penalty Corner outfit, the three goals from field play rank it ninth in the 16-team tournament.
On India’s lack of field goals, Fulton said, “It’s a [matter of] small composure. They play a certain way, and one team plays man-to-man, one team plays zonal, which puts seven players, eight players in the D.
“That’s a different approach to playing if there were three in the D. We’ve got different plans for both teams, but at the same time, we’ve got to implement our plan.”

title: My temperament is suitable for red-ball cricket: Sanat
content:
In decades gone by, the Duleep Trophy was considered as a stepping stone for players aiming to break into the Indian Test team. Even though the zonal competition no longer retains that allure, getting picked for the season-opener is a considerable boost for the top performers of the previous Ranji Trophy campaign.
Ask Sanat Sangwan. The Delhi opener grabbed eyeballs in the 2025-26 Ranji season, racking up 828 runs — third in the list of highest scorers behind Karnataka’s R. Smaran and teammate Ayush Doseja — in 14 innings at an average of 69. The 25-year-old has been deservedly rewarded with a spot in the North Zone squad, which begins its Duleep Trophy campaign against West Zone at the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru on Sunday.
Although Sanat will go into the First Class tournament on the back of playing T20 cricket in the Delhi Premier League, the left-hander’s preparation in recent weeks had covered all bases.
“Along with playing in the DPL, I had been practising against the red ball. To do well in red-ball cricket, you have to work harder. It is a more difficult format for openers since we have to face the new ball. I tend to prepare more for red-ball cricket in the off-season,” Sanat said during a media interaction in the National capital.
During the course of Sanat’s prolific run-making exploits last season, his propensity to wear down bowling attacks was impressive. The youngster, who counts Virat Kohli and Lewis Hamilton among his sporting idols, prides himself on his patience in the longest format.
“My temperament has been suitable for red-ball cricket from the outset. I look to ensure that my shot-selection is in sync with how I’ve prepared,” he mentioned. “I don’t play a cover drive in the first hour. I don’t play away from my body. You can still get out, but the chances reduce. It frustrates bowlers. Once you are set, you can open up.”

title: Badminton World championships: Treesa and Gayatri continue dream run, ensure maiden medal
content:
When in doubt, attack. Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand stuck to the mantra regardless of the scoreline and reaped the rewards, assuring themselves of a maiden medal at the badminton World championships here on Friday.
Their 16-21, 21-15, 21-13 victory against the Chinese World No. 4 Jia Yifan & Zhang Shuxian in the quarterfinals at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium came in 70 minutes. It was their third big scalp in as many matches after ousting the World No. 17 and World No. 7 pairs earlier.
In the process, the unseeded, unfancied duo also became the first Indian women’s pair to do make it to the Worlds semifinals since Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa’s historic bronze in 2011. In fact that medal started India’s streak of winning at least one medal in every edition since then.
It would also be the only medal for India this time after two-time bronze medallists Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty lost to the World No. 3 Chinese pair of Wei Keng Liang and Chang Wang 21-18, 21-9 in just 35 minutes.
Ranked 39th, Treesa and Gayatri trailed 6-0 in the opening game before fighting back to close the gap to 9-8. They eventually lost 21-16 but at no point did it look like they were ready to give up.
Gayatri being quick and busy on the net, smashed cross-court winners and constantly set Treesa up for the winners.
The two went from 7-10 to 13-10 in the second game and, with nothing to lose, pushed hard. They cut down the unforced errors and kept it tight, forcing Yifan, a four time World champion and the reigning Olympic champion, to conceding points and took the match into the decider.
Thereafter it was India all the way. Treesa and Gayatri raced to an 11-5 lead before change of ends and closed out the tie 21-13.
Satwik and Chirag, meanwhile, had their chances in the opening game and even led 18-16 before the opponents reeled off five points to win 21-18. The flat drives targeting the Indians’ bodies meant Satwik and Chirag were always cramped for space.
Wei and Chang’s lightening quick returns, coupled with retrievals from all over the court made it impossible for Satwik and Chiraj to either lift or fall back on their trademark smashes to get points as the Chinese wrapped up the match in quick time.

title: Premier League 2026-27: Champions Arsenal embrace being 'hunted' as new season begins
content:
Mikel Arteta said Arsenal will embrace being "hunted" by their title rivals as the new Premier League season kicks off with the champion facing Coventry on Friday (August 21, 2026).
Just 34 days after a captivating World Cup came to an end, the Premier League returns with Arsenal aiming to cement their position as English football's preeminent force.
The Gunners have the honour of playing the opening game of the season at the Emirates Stadium, before a packed slate of top-flight matches across Saturday, Sunday and Monday.
Arteta's side won the Premier League for the first time in 22 years last season, finally getting their hands on the trophy after finishing as runners-up for the previous three years.
Installed as the bookmakers' title favourites this term, Arsenal look well placed to reign supreme again, especially given the questions surrounding their title challengers.
They routed Manchester City 3-0 in the Community Shield last weekend to send a statement of intent to the chasing pack.
Bolstered by new signings Bruno Guimaraes and Christos Tzolis, with Ezri Konsa set to join from Aston Villa, Arteta has no doubts Arsenal can cope with the pressure of being the team everyone wants to beat.
"We start from scratch, from zero, and we're going to have to prove we are at the level to go back to that position again," he said.
"We need to show that desire, and the ambition to be better than what we were last season, a month ago, a week ago.
"If you give me the choice, I want to be first, I want to be hunted, and I want to be in control of our future, rather than depending on somebody else."
Winning the Premier League was a cathartic moment for the north London club after so many near-misses raised doubts about their character.
‘A long marathon’
Arteta believes surviving that test of their resolve will stand them in good stead in their bid to win Arsenal's first back-to-back titles since the 1930s.
"We need to breathe because it's going to be a long marathon," he said.
"We have the ability to improve, to evolve, and that's what I sense and I feel around the club, especially around the players."
Lampard’s Coventry ready for ‘reality’
Coventry are back in the Premier League for the first time in 25 years after winning promotion from the Championship.
After a spell in the fourth tier in 2017-18 and twice being force to ground-share with other clubs after financial issues involving their own stadium, Coventry's return to the elite is a feel-good story.
But even Sky Blues manager Frank Lampard acknowledges the uplifting tale might not have a happy ending.
"We will go through tougher times this year for sure because of the competition we're up against now," Lampard said.
"It's just a reality that we need to be ready for."
New managers at big clubs
Manchester City, runners-up last season, start life without Pep Guardiola at home to Bournemouth on Sunday.
Guardiola stepped down at the end of last season after winning 20 trophies in a glorious decade at the Etihad Stadium.
Former Chelsea manager Enzo Maresca has accepted the daunting task of emulating the Spaniard's success.
Liverpool's new manager Andoni Iraola will take charge of his first game in Sunday's trip to Newcastle.
Ex-Bournemouth boss Iraola was hired by Liverpool to replace Arne Slot, who was sacked following the Reds' disappointing fifth-place finish last season.
Xabi Alonso begins his reign as Chelsea boss with a west London derby at Fulham on Monday.
Manchester United start on Saturday at promoted Hull, who are back in the top tier for the first time since 2017.
Big-spending Tottenham, who narrowly avoided relegation last season, travel to Brentford on Saturday.
Europa League winners Aston Villa, ravaged by a host of star departures since last season, head to Brighton on Sunday.
