title: What India must do against Australia to qualify for Women's Hockey World Cup semis? Full scenario explained
content:
What India must do against Australia to qualify for Women's Hockey World Cup semis? Full scenario explained
Women's Hockey World Cup: India will take on Australia on Sunday. Here's the full semi-finals qualification scenario.
India’s hopes of reaching the semi-finals of the FIH Women’s Hockey World Cup 2026 have ultimately come down to the final day of Pool E matches after facing a 0-2 defeat to the Netherlands on August 21. The latest result for Sjoerd Marijne's side complicated the race for the last-four spots, and it's a race to the finish for all four teams involved - India, China, Netherlands and Australia. The Indian women’s hockey team now has one match remaining in the second round, with Australia awaiting them on Sunday, August 23.
India currently have one point, the same as Australia, while the Netherlands have already secured their place in the semi-finals after beating India. The top two teams from Pool E will advance to the semi-finals.
Also Read: India all but out of the semi-finals race after losing to Netherlands in Men's Hockey World Cup
That leaves India with a straightforward target but a potentially complicated qualification equation: they need to beat Australia and then hope the Netherlands-China result goes their way, or produce a strong enough result against Australia to win the relevant tie-breaker if China also finish on four points.
The second round began with India and China each carrying 1 point from their 0-0 draw in the first round. The Netherlands entered the pool with three points after finishing top of Pool A, while Australia came through with no points carried forward.
The Netherlands then defeated India 2-0, taking their tally to six points and confirming their qualification for the semi-finals. India remain on one point, while China have one point from their opening second-round fixture.
What does India need to do?
A victory over Australia would take India to four points. That would put the Indian side in a strong position to finish among the top two. However, qualification would not be mathematically guaranteed in every scenario.
If the Netherlands beat or draws with China, India would finish ahead of China and secure second place. But if China defeat the Netherlands, they too would move to four points. India and China could then finish level on points, making the tournament's tie-breaking criteria crucial.
Under the FIH regulations, teams level on points are separated first by the number of matches won, then by goal difference, goals scored, and finally by the head-to-head result, among other criteria. India and China drew 0-0 in their first-round meeting, meaning the head-to-head result would not immediately separate them if they remain level after the earlier criteria.
That makes the margin of victory in both final matches potentially important.
What if India draw against Australia?
A draw would leave India on two points. Their qualification would then depend heavily on the Netherlands-China match. If China lose to the Netherlands, China would remain on one point, and India would move into second place with two points.
However, if China draws with or defeats the Netherlands, China would finish with at least two points and could remain ahead of India, depending on the final standings and tie-break criteria. Therefore, a draw would leave India vulnerable and would take the qualification decision out of their own hands.
What if India lose?
A defeat would leave India on one point and effectively end their hopes of reaching the semi-finals. Australia would move to four points, while China would also remain in contention for the second qualification spot. India would then have no route into the top two under the possible final standings.
For India, therefore, the message is clear: a win against Australia is the safest route to keeping their semi-final campaign alive.

title: Pullela Gopichand explains Treesa-Gayatri's World Championships breakthrough
content:
NEW DELHI: Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand's run to a historic bronze medal at the 
BWF World Championships
 was no accident. It was the result of six weeks of targeted work, tactical tweaks and an unwavering emphasis on patience, said chief national coach 
Pullela Gopichand
 on Saturday.
The Indian women's doubles team signed off with a bronze medal after going down to defending champions Liu Sheng Shu and Tan Ning of China 21-18, 13-21, 8-21 in front a massive crowd at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium.
Jolly-Gopichand, both 23, became India's first women's doubles World Championships medallists in 15 years.
Later, as India's campaign ended with a solitary medal, Gopichand spoke to the media about the technical changes that transformed their game, the significance of Gayatri's achievement, and why the pair's breakthrough could be another step forward for Indian badminton ahead of the 
Asian Games
 in Japan.
Excerpts:
Q. About the women's doubles semi-final. Till the second game, they were quite there in the match. What changed?Gopichand: I think until the second game mid-part they were in the match. Suddenly, they didn't contact the shuttle as much as I would have really liked. And then, they just lost it. But also, credit to the Chinese girls, because they were serving very well.
Because there was a good amount of spin and tumble on the serve. 
And then, on the first return, they were hitting very hard. So, I think Gayatri's and Treesa's chance of getting on the attack from the very beginning was not happening. But overall, I'm happy with the way they have played.
New Delhi, Aug 22 (ANI): India's Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand Pullela during the women's doubles semifinal at the BWF Badminton World Championships at Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium, in New Delhi on Saturday. (ANI Photo/Naveen Sharma)
 I think once they lost the attack as much because they were not contacting it or the grip was there, which was very difficult. They've got a tumble on the serve which was very distinct. So what was happening in that moment, you push it, the next return was very fast.
And then you were engaging in the parallel game as much. So in my book, I think you don't have too many options. The one option you could do was just lift the first serve and then start blocking or counter-attacking from the smash. That's one.
But then, when you are under three-point deficit, then that becomes very difficult to be calm and execute that strategy. So in that sense, I'm okay with it. In the sense, you have to battle that. You can't run away from it. When people push the pace, you have to get used to it.
Q. After the high of winning and beating the Chinese, how difficult was it to come today or what did you have to tell the girls to kind of get back to focusing on the next challenge?Gopichand:
 I think they did well. Of course, they must have been excited here or when they got back. But I think overall, by the time they reached the hotel, I think the recovery had started. And food and rest and off their phones. So, all those basic hygiene things were done. And they prepared well. Yes, they couldn't win today but overall it was good.
Q. Can you shed some light on what helped the duo this week? What were the keys to their success this week?Gopichand: I think overall they have a naturally good game. Decent serve, both of them serve well. Smash-wise, Treesa is very good. Gayatri is very strong at the net. They get those rhythms, patches of rhythms, which they've been very, very good at. And I think the atmosphere and the stadium is also, it's a big hall, right? So you can see some very long matches happening. So you can't just get a point. You have to earn a point. So you can't just be in a hurry and play a stroke to get a point. You have to work yourself. So patience is something which is spoken about. And basically it just means that you can't be in a hurry. You have to be quick, you have to be fast, but not necessarily in a hurry. And that's what patience would mean. And at the end of it, to get back and stick to your strategy is worth saving.
Whatever we've worked in the last six weeks has helped. And it's good to see when the practice which you do actually gives you dividends on court.
Gopichand
New Delhi, Aug 22 (ANI): India's Gayatri Gopichand Pullela in action against China's Liu Sheng Shu and Tan Ning in the women's doubles semifinal during the BWF Badminton World Championships at Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium, in New Delhi on Saturday. (ANI Photo/Naveen Sharma)
 We've worked on it. And I think it's whatever we've worked in the last six weeks has helped. And it's good to see when the practice which you do actually gives you dividends on court. All of these things we've worked on.
I think it's a revelation how Treesa kept charging at the net and started taking control. Gayatri's backcourt has been good. And the rhythm on her serve was very good. I think these two aspects. And at the crucial moments, they were able to pull through.
Whenever my players have played, I think I've always had the same feeling. And there's no extra for Gayatri
Gopichand
 Well, to be honest, I don't know if I can articulate it in that sense. But I think whenever my players have played, I think I've always had the same feeling. And there's no extra for Gayatri. More than I've had for any of my players.
With God's grace, in a family... there are two Arjuna awardees. Two players, two Arjuna awardees. It's rare.
Gopichand
 I'm very proud of the way she's played. With God's grace, in a family... there are two Arjuna awardees. Two players, two Arjuna awardees. It's rare. I'm grateful to God for this. And yes, I'm very proud of her performance and her results. And the way she's conducted herself.
Q. Gopi sir, a word on India's campaign at the BWF World Championships?Gopichand: Overall, it has been a little unfortunate that we have lost some close matches. In women's singles, we have lost both the matches very closely. In men's singles, Ayush's first day was very good. But the second day was a little bit disappointing. But overall, I think we were decent in that sense. I won't be too worried about it. Some days, these things do happen. But the next time around, at the Asian Games, I'm hoping for better performance.
Q. How is the Indian badminton team going to prepare for the Asian Games? What specific areas are you going to look at as a coach?Gopichand: Well, I think as of now, what's happening is that each one has a dedicated team allotted to them. So we have Lakshya (Sen), we have Ayush (Shetty), we have (Kidambi) Srikanth or Tharun (Mannepalli). Or whether it's the girls - PV Sindhu, Unnati (Hooda), Tanvi (Sharma), Devika (Sihag). All of them have a dedicated team. So they get back to work. Some of them are playing tournaments. They play the China Open. So I think they're all now in a stage of their career that they're all professional in that sense.
 They have a team to work along. So we get along and move on to the Asian Games.
Also to just make a point, the team is really pumped up. Whether it's Thomas Cup, I think the players themselves do a lot of work to get together and build the camaraderie in that sense. So that's what we're hoping will happen.
Q. We have won medals in men's singles, women's singles, men's doubles and women's doubles. Not yet in mixed doubles. What do you make of it?Gopichand:
 I'm glad we're asking these questions (in this manner). Because when Saina (Nehwal) went on in 2008 when she reached the quarters. So the question was, where are the men? And then where's the men's doubles? The women's doubles? So we're just ticking one box at a time. And hopefully mixed doubles will be the next one.

title: Erasmus vows Springboks can still win series after Ellis Park rout by All Blacks
content:
Erasmus vows Springboks can still win series after Ellis Park rout by All Blacks
JOHANNESBURG — Coach Rassie Erasmus reassured South Africa supporters that recent history proved the test series against New Zealand can still be won after losing the opening salvo 33-16 on Saturday.
The All Blacks' biggest ever win at Ellis Park stripped double world champion South Africa of its No. 1 test ranking and ended the Springboks' 12-test win streak, their longest under Erasmus.
They have three more tests in their first full-scale series in 30 years and go to Cape Town next Saturday.
“We have been in many catastrophic situations in our lives,” Erasmus said.
He noted they lost the first test against the British and Irish Lions in 2021 and won that three-test series. He also noted losing their opening pool game to New Zealand at the 2019 Rugby World Cup and winning the trophy.
“There is a way out, and that's winning three matches on the trot,” Erasmus said. "Without doubt, it puts them in a very good position which they thoroughly deserve.
“We were thoroughly beaten by a team that is now No. 1 in the world — it'll be nice to go into the next game as the underdogs,” he quipped.
"We were dominant in the scrums but it doesn't help you if you're dominant in one or two parts of the game. The All Blacks were more dominant in most parts of the game.
“I'm not going to butter it up with that cliché and say we're going to learn from this and get better. We didn't need to learn from this; we knew what we had to do on the day — we didn’t do it.”
The Springboks failed to convert numerous chances in a dominant first half and turned with only a 13-12 lead. New Zealand was courageous and clinical and remarkably cantered home by five tries to one.
The key moment was near the hour mark when the Boks trailed 19-16 and had a scrum in front of the All Blacks' posts. Then they conceded a penalty on their own feed.
“Even if we had kicked over that scrum penalty and we won we still made a hell of a lot of errors,” Erasmus said. "But it wasn't a wake-up call. There were just so many things that we did wrong and that New Zealand did right — so I'm not going to say we learnt a lot of things from this match.
"There would have been a lot of things we'd have to put right even if we had scratched through this match with a one-point win.
“We didn't play well. There were a lot of things we didn't convert. New Zealand forced those on to us by being really intense and sharp.”
In regard to injuries, his main concerns were wingers Cheslin Kolbe and Kurt-Lee Arendse.
Arendse failed a head check after his mouthguard pinged in the first half. A mandatory stand-down for concussion made Arendse a doubt for the second test in Cape Town next weekend. Kolbe left in the second half with suspected cramp, Erasmus said.
Kolbe was perfect off the tee with four from four, and goalkicked ahead of Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu because, Erasmus said, he's “our most accurate kicker."

title: What team does Tyreek Hill play for in 2026? Is he retired? Latest NFL status
content:
What team does Tyreek Hill play for in 2026? Is he retired? Latest NFL status
Miami Dolphins released Tyreek Hill in February 2026 as part of a major roster reset.
Free-agent wide receiver Tyreek Hill is not expected to sign with an NFL team before the start of the 2026 regular season, his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, said Friday.
What happened to Tyreek Hill?
Tyreek Hill, 32, has remained unsigned since the Miami Dolphins released him in February as part of a major roster reset.
He is still recovering from a serious left knee injury suffered in Week 4 of the 2025 season against the New York Jets. Hill dislocated his knee and tore multiple ligaments, including his ACL and LCL. The injury ended his season after just four games.
What did his agent say?
Drew Rosenhaus appeared on The Pat McAfee Show and said Hill is making progress but is not ready to return.
"I don't expect Tyreek to sign before the season," Rosenhaus said on Friday. "He sent me a video yesterday, this is good timing, of him running hills and he looked great. I said to him, 'you look great' and he said to me, 'I still have some work to do. I'm not ready yet.'"
Rosenhaus said he is not putting pressure on Hill or setting a deadline for his return.
"I think what I have said to Tyreek is take your time," Rosenhaus added. "It's not when you come back, it's how you come back. We want you to come back when you feel your best. There's no sense of urgency timing-wise, I think this is a future Hall of Famer who still has a lot of good football left in him. This was a devastating injury, but everyone's gonna be so impressed when they see how well Tyreek is rehabbing."
Rosenhaus believes Hill could still make a big impact later in the season, particularly for a team making a playoff push.
"It's not hyperbole for me to predict that he will play this season, when I'm not sure," Rosenhaus said. "But I do think when he does sign, he will be a coveted player. He'll be the kind of guy that will impact the playoff race and will certainly be successful once he signs."
Also Read: Why did Nick Chubb retire? Net worth in focus as NFL player ends career at 30
Has Tyreek Hill talked about retirement?
Despite his injury and off-field issues, Hill has not indicated that he plans to retire.
In an interview with People in February, Hill said he was walking without a brace and remained focused on football and his family.
"My focus right now is just playing ball and spending time with my kids and just doing what I'm best at: providing for my family," Hill said at the time. "So all the noise, I feel like if you allow that kind of stuff to get in the way of what you're trying to do, it can only cloud what you're really trying to get accomplished."
In September last year, Hill was accused of several domestic violence-related incidents by his estranged wife, Keeta Vaccaro.

title: Dodgers put CF Andy Pages (hand) on IL, recall CF Alek Thomas
content:
Dodgers put CF Andy Pages (hand) on IL, recall CF Alek Thomas
BASEBALL-MLB-LAD-PAGES-THOMAS/
One day after suffering a left hand fracture, Los Angeles Dodgers All-Star center fielder Andy Pages was placed on the 10-day injured list, with center fielder Alek Thomas recalled from Triple-A Oklahoma City on Saturday to fill his spot.
Pages, 25, is expected to miss at least a month after he was hit by a pitch on the back of his left hand on Friday by Pittsburgh Pirates right-hander Bubba Chandler in the Dodgers' 5-4, 10-inning home victory. Pages was hit by the pitch in the third but remained in the game until he was replaced in the outfield by Enrique Hernandez in the fifth.
"It's not season-ending because things like are four to five weeks," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said postgame. "I would expect him back, knowing him, on the earlier side. It will be four weeks, but there is time in the season for him to be back."
Pages is batting .272 with a .338 on-base percentage, a .458 slugging percentage, 21 home runs and 80 RBIs in 128 games this season.
Along with Thomas, the right-handed-hitting Hernandez and switch-hitting Tommy Edman are expected to help out in center over the next month.
An All-Star this year for the first time in his third season, Pages is a career .265/.319/.445 hitter with 61 home runs and 212 RBIs in 400 games.
Thomas, 26, was acquired from the Diamondbacks on May 12 for minor-leaguer Jose Requena and has yet to make his Dodgers debut. A second-round pick by Arizona in the 2018 draft, Thomas was hitting .181 with two home runs and 10 RBIs in 28 games this season at the time of the trade.
Over parts of five seasons, all with the Diamondbacks, Thomas is a .230 hitter with 31 home runs and 143 RBIs in 448 games.

title: Is Brenda Song married to Macaulay Culkin? All about their relationship and kids as she makes NFL analyst debut
content:
Is Brenda Song married to Macaulay Culkin? All about their relationship and kids as she makes NFL analyst debut
Brenda Song has spoken about the close bond she shares with Macaulay Culkin, describing him as someone she can rely on beyond their romantic relationship.
Actress Brenda Song has previously caught the attention of NFL fans with her strong understanding of football, and she is now preparing to take that connection a step further with her broadcasting debut.
Brenda Song set for NFL analyst debut
The 38-year-old actress is set to join CBS’ coverage of the Los Angeles Rams’ preseason matchup against the New Orleans Saints on Saturday as a guest color analyst. Song will contribute to the broadcast during the third quarter.
A California native, Song has long identified as a passionate Los Angeles sports fan and has been vocal about her support for the Rams.
Her interest in the team and knowledge of the sport have made her a familiar name among the franchise’s fanbase.
As Song gets ready for her first appearance in an NFL broadcast booth, here is a closer look at her personal life, including her partner Macaulay Culkin..
Also read | Jake Bobo injury update: Bad news for Seahawks as WR lands on season-ending IR
Is Brenda Song married?
Brenda Song is not legally married at this point, but she has been in a long-standing relationship with her fiancé, actor Macaulay Culkin.
The pair reportedly met briefly in 2014, although their relationship did not begin until several years later. They grew closer in 2017 while working together on the comedy-drama Changeland, which was filmed in Thailand.
When Culkin and Song got engaged
After keeping their relationship largely private for years, Culkin proposed to Song in January 2022, and the couple became engaged. Song previously opened up about their unexpected romance during an interview with Access Hollywood.
“I think that’s what was so beautiful. I always say he’s like my unicorn. I wasn’t going to settle for anything, but he is exactly what I was hoping to look for,” she said at the time.
Also read | Is Ed Oliver married? Bills defensive tackle's family and kids in focus amid 2-year-old son's death
Song has also spoken about the close bond she shares with Culkin, describing him as someone she can rely on beyond their romantic relationship.
“He understands my work, we can talk about football, we talk about basketball, we can cook together. I think I just really lucked out,” she added.
The couple share two kids
The couple have also started a family together and are parents to two sons.
Their first child, Dakota, was born in April 2021 and was named after Culkin’s late sister. They later welcomed their second son, Carson, in 2022.

title: Jake Bobo injury update: Bad news for Seahawks as WR lands on season-ending IR
content:
Jake Bobo injury update: Bad news for Seahawks as WR lands on season-ending IR
Jake Bobo’s placement on injured reserve opens a spot on Seattle’s roster, and the Seahawks moved quickly to bring in another wide receiver.
The Seattle Seahawks have suffered a major setback with less than three weeks remaining before the start of the 2026 NFL season.
WR Jake Bobo lands on season-ending IR
Wide receiver Jake Bobo has been placed on injured reserve following a significant knee injury sustained during Friday’s joint practice with the Tennessee Titans.
ESPN reporter Adam Schefter confirmed the development, revealing that Bobo’s injury will keep him out for the entire season.
"Seahawks placed WR Jake Bobo on season-ending injured reserve, the result of the significant knee injury he suffered during Friday’s joint practice with the Titans," Schefter tweeted on X.
The 28-year-old has recorded 34 receptions for 323 yards and three touchdowns during his NFL career. He was expected to provide valuable depth at wide receiver for Seattle this season.
Also read | Why did Nick Chubb retire? Net worth in focus as NFL player ends career at 30
The Seattle No. 19 suffered the knee injury while attempting to make a leaping catch during Friday’s practice.
Bobo’s offseason contract saga
Bobo entered the offseason as a restricted free agent, prompting the Seahawks to place an original-round tender worth $3.5 million on him.
The Jacksonville Jaguars subsequently signed him to a two-year, $5.5 million offer sheet that included $4.5 million in guaranteed money, but Seattle chose to match the offer and retain the receiver.
Who will replace Jake Bobo?
Bobo’s placement on injured reserve opens a spot on Seattle’s roster, and the Seahawks moved quickly to bring in another wide receiver. The team signed Julian Hicks to fill the vacancy created by Bobo’s absence.
Also read | Is Ed Oliver married? Bills defensive tackle's family and kids in focus amid 2-year-old son's death
Schefter also confirmed the roster move in the same update, writing, "Seattle signed WR Julian Hicks to fill the open roster spot," the ESPN reporter mentioned in his tweet.
Hicks gets another Seahawks chance
Hicks is returning to Seattle after initially joining the Seahawks last weekend. He was later waived when the team needed a roster spot for the addition of Trevon Diggs.
The 26-year-old went undrafted out of Albany in 2024 and subsequently signed with the Green Bay Packers.

He spent his rookie season on Green Bay’s practice squad before returning to the Packers and participating in their training camp and preseason the following year.

title: Kuldeep or Saransh? The subplot thickens as Colombo braces for a different script
content:
TimesofIndia.com in Colombo:
 Will he, won't he? Questions surrounding 
Kuldeep Yadav
 reached a fever pitch when the chinaman stayed away from the second training session in a row. While the official word from the Indian camp was that he was being rested from the first session, KL Rahul, who was also absent on Friday, turned up for a hit on Saturday.
Kuldeep staying confined to the hotel room further raised eyebrows, as this is highly unusual, especially for an away fixture and particularly when he has bowled only 25 overs in the Galle Test. For a bowler who hardly missed training even when benched for all the Tests in England last summer, his absence in Colombo turned attention to 
Saransh Jain
.
The 33-year-old got a good workout on both days, and his routine on the eve of the match has only thickened the subplot. Moments after reaching the ground, he went straight to the pitch to visualise before moving to the practice surface. Giving him company was Team India's spin bowling coach 
Sairaj Bahutule
, and the duo spent some time talking and doing spot bowling before it was Saransh's turn to put the pads on.
The left-hander switched nets and faced different combinations of net bowlers and throwdown specialists, watched by both head coach Gautam Gambhir and men's senior selection committee chairman Ajit Agarkar. The moment his batting session ended, Gambhir had a long chat with Saransh and even gave him a pat on the chest before the off-spinner left for the dressing room.
India's Saransh Jain during a practice session ahead of the second Test cricket match between India and Sri Lanka, in Colombo. (PTI) 
Not just the cues from India's final net session, but Sri Lanka's addition of left-handers also points more strongly towards Saransh. 
Home captain Dhananjaya de Silva confirmed that Kamil Mishara, a left-hander, will take the opener's slot, and there is also the option of Sahan Arachchige, another southpaw, for the middle order.
Gambhir kept his playing XI cards close to his chest at the pre-match press conference but asserted that the focus will be on assembling a bowling attack which gives them 20 wickets. Whether it will feature Saransh or Kuldeep wasn't revealed, but "all options" are open.
We know how good a bowler Kuldeep is. And more importantly, sometimes, it's up to the captain as well, where he feels that if his two other spinners can get him wickets, looking at the conditions, what pace he wants a certain spinner to bow
Gautam Gambhir
"We will try and pick the best bowling attack which will get us 20 wickets. You can score 1000 runs in Test cricket, there is no guarantee you are going to win a Test match but if you get 20 wickets, you have all the probability and possibility of winning the Test match. We will try and take the best attack that can get you 20 wickets, whether you have got three left-arm spinners in it or an offie or three seamers - we will have all our options open," said Gambhir.
In the Galle Test, Kuldeep wasn't captain Shubman Gill's preferred option as he played the role of a third spinner in an attack also featuring Manav Suthar and Ravindra Jadeja. The two finger spinners did the bulk of the bowling, and Gambhir reiterated that it was all about "getting the result".
India's Kuldeep Yadav appeals for an unsuccessful wicket on day three of the first test cricket match between India and Sri Lanka, in Galle, Sri Lanka. (PTI)
"Ultimately, we know how good a bowler Kuldeep is. And more importantly, sometimes, it's up to the captain as well, where he feels that if his two other spinners can get him wickets, looking at the conditions, what pace he wants a certain spinner to bowl. And it's not about guys underbowling and it's about getting the result. For me, I think that is more important," explained Gambhir.
"When you play five proper bowlers, someone will eventually get under-bowled. And that is what Test cricket is all about. It's not about someone not delivering and getting under-bowled. It's about who the captain feels or the management feel can be the most threatening in that particular condition," he added.
I think the conversation I have had with Kuldeep is just bowl your good spell rather than looking desperate to take wickets.
Gautam Gambhir
Kuldeep was far from threatening across the two innings in Galle, returning with only one wicket. Bahutule revealed that Kuldeep was adapting and making changes based on the role assigned to him. Both Gambhir and Bahutule backed the chinaman, and the head coach revealed a very interesting conversation he had with the 31-year-old after the fixture.
India's Kuldeep Yadav bowls on the third day of the first test match between India and Sri Lanka at Galle International Stadium, in Galle on Monday. (ANI Photo)
"I think the conversation I have had with Kuldeep is just bowl your good spell rather than looking desperate to take wickets. Because sometimes, as a wrist spinner, when you are looking and you are desperate to take wickets, I think your control can go away as well. We rate Kuldeep very highly and we know how successful and how threatening he can be in every condition given to him. But again, I think the same thing, as I said, that we're going to try and pick the best type of what can deliver in these conditions," said Gambhir.
There were no direct revelations, but plenty of undertones and cues have only increased the intrigue around Kuldeep vs Saransh.

title: France’s badminton surge gathers pace with Alex Lanier
content:
France’s badminton surge gathers pace with Alex Lanier
The 21-year-old made it to the men’s singles final at the World Championships here beating Victor Lai in a high-quality draining contest
New Delhi: France has been the talk of the badminton world since last year, when three of its players—Alex Lanier, Christo Popov, and Toma Popov Junior — announced their arrival on the big stage and advanced to the third round of the BWF World Championships in Paris. Denmark has been traditional powerhouse of the sport in Europe, but a gust of fresh wind was blowing. At the BWF Worlds here, that gust of wind has turned into a raging storm sweeping through the sport.
That was evident at the Thomas Cup, the prestigious world team championships, where France stunned teams such as Indonesia, Japan and India to reach the final. They eventually lost to China, but for a team that had never previously reached the quarter-finals, it was as big an achievement as it gets. It came on the back of France’s victory at the European Men’s Team Championships, where they beat Denmark.
On Saturday, Alex Lanier scripted another first for France, reaching the World Championships final with a brilliant come-from-behind win over promising Canadian Victor Lai in the semi-finals. His medal will be the first by a French shuttler at the World Championships.
All through the week, the 21-year-old world No.10 Lanier has played like he is on a mission, taking out former world champion Kunlavut Vitidsarn in the quarter-finals. In both matches, Lanier was a game down but showed tremendous temperament and fighting spirit to turn the tables. His physical capabilities were particularly striking, especially after two draining, high-pressure matches on the biggest stage.
Few emotions were on display as Lanier remained focused on the final, where he will meet Japan’s Kodai Naraoka, who stopped the gallant run of 36-year-old Chou Tien-chen 17-21, 21-11, 21-10.
“I don’t feel that emotional at the moment. I think I’m a little bit too tired, but I’m also proud of the way I managed that match (semi-final). Also, mentally, I’m not really thinking how big it is,” Lanier said.
“We haven’t done the tournament yet, so definitely I don’t want to think about the historical aspect. I just enjoy being on court and playing my best, so that’s my main priority at the moment.”
Lanier’s physical preparation in the build-up helped him pull off such long matches. Against Kunlavut, who has reached the last three finals, he was on court for an hour and 18 minutes. Against Victor, it was an hour and 25 minutes of a gruelling contest. Towards the home stretch, Lanier’s superior physical conditioning saw him through, even as the draining match began to take a toll on Victor.
“We prepared well, especially physically, before the Japan Open. We prepared to be ready, and we knew that it’s going to be very physical, a World Championship.
“And it has been definitely physically demanding. And then we just went, we just polished a little bit of my game. We went to Denmark to get the intensity, to get some very good practice,” said Lanier.
Three French players are now in the top 15 of the men’s singles world rankings. The rise has led every nation to sit back and take notice of France’s growing presence on the international badminton stage.
Sitting behind Lanier during the match was Kęstutis Navickas, the Lithuanian Olympian and singles head coach of the French national badminton team.
“It’s a long-term work by the French Federation that is giving results now,” said Kęstutis. “The French Federation has been working for many years to create the system and the structure. And now we are in a privileged position that the structure started creating the players. When we have the competition like we have now in men’s singles, we are pushing each other,” he added.
“We are learning from each other. And that gives the benefit to each of the players and to French badminton.”

title: India's World Cup hopes hang by a thread after Netherlands turn three sharp moments into a crushing 3-1 victory
content:
India's World Cup hopes hang by a thread after Netherlands turn three sharp moments into a crushing 3-1 victory
In a crucial match, Netherlands defeated India 3-1 in the Hockey World Cup, securing a semi-final spot while India's hopes dimmed.
Mumbai: Near the centre of the pitch, Jorrit Croon stretched out to intercept a loose pass, five minutes from the final hooter. Then he charged forward, shrugging off the challenge of experienced India defender Amit Rohidas. A quick look to his left and he sent a measured low cross to an unmarked Thijs van Dam.
The first touch got the ball into the circle. The second – with a hint of showboating – was a little dink over the onrushing Indian goalkeeper HS Mohith. And then came the finish into an open goal.
That finish wrapped up co-hosts Netherlands’ 3-1 win over India in the Hockey World Cup second group stage fixture on Saturday. And the final goal served perhaps as that one moment of play best summarising the well-attended match at the Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen.
With the win, Netherlands secured their semi-final spot, leaving India’s hopes all but over. The defeat dimmed India’s hopes as it took qualification out of their hands. Not having taken any point from the preliminary group stage – England (they beat India) and the Dutch have – further diminished India’s chances.
India held on to most of the possession – 61.6 percent to Netherlands’ 38.4. India had more circle entries (20 to 16) and more penalty corners (7 to 4). But it was the Dutch who were better organized and made the most of those small moments that came their way to score.
Playing against the reigning Olympic champions and world No.1 team is no easy matter. Yet India needed to get a positive result to stay within reach of a semi-final spot.
India did start the game well as they held possession and made a few forays into the opposition shooting circle before the Dutch could get any true touch of the ball. As the minutes slipped by though, the hosts found their rhythm and started to build, allowing India time on the ball while themselves looking for those sharp moves.
So disciplined and patient were the Dutch in defence that they did not concede a penalty corner in the first two quarters.
After that, the Dutch started to turn up the pressure. They started to win the individual battles more frequently. The midfield was being bossed more by Justen Blok and Derck de Vilder than Hardik Singh and Manpreet Singh. Jarmanpreet Singh was falling a foot behind Terrence Pieters while India captain and drag-flick star Harmanpreet Singh seemed to be struggling with an injury.
Abhishek, India’s in-form striker who had been weaving through defenders in the previous matches, was being kept quiet by Floris Wortelboer (the player of the match) and Lars Balk.
With the individual battles aced, the Dutch started to make their moves into the opposition half. In the 41st minute, they found the breakthrough when Tijmen Reyenga’s attempted shot was mishit, but fell kindly to Duco Telgenkamp, who deflected it past Suraj Karkera (in goal at the time).
Trailing, India started to put more pressure on the Dutch defence, but the hosts quelled the danger without fuss. Goalkeeper Derk Meijer needed to make two important stops, including a superb stick save off a powerfully struck Sanjay drag-flick.
On the break once again in the 51st minute, De Vilder lofted a pass forward to Koen Bijen, who controlled expertly before sending a driven pass into the shooting circle. Tjep Hoedemakers was the first to react, and with the ball at least a foot in the air, he cleverly deflected into the India goal to double the lead.
Harmanpreet managed to pull one back and give India some hope with his sixth goal of the tournament in the 52nd minute – a powerful drag-flick placed hard and low, well away from a diving Meijer.
Immediately after that, Harmanpreet was seen rushing into the dugout for treatment, while his teammates tried to search for an equaliser.
That hope was quashed three minutes later with Van Dam’s goal.
“The first three quarters, we played well. We managed to hold the ball and defensively we did well,” a dejected Harmanpreet told FIH after the match. “But for the entire 60 minutes, we have to stay focused and consistent. In the last quarter we made the same mistakes, and (Netherlands) picked up and scored from those mistakes.”

title: After World Championships, Pullela Gopichand lays out India’s Asian Games plan: 'We are ticking one box at a time'
content:
After World Championships, Pullela Gopichand lays out India’s Asian Games plan: 'We are ticking one box at a time'
Coach Pullela Gopichand aims for focused training ahead of the Asian Games after Gayatri Gopichand and Treesa Jolly earned women’s doubles bronze
Following a gritty campaign at the BWF World Championships that culminated in a historic women’s doubles bronze for Gayatri Gopichand and Treesa Jolly, chief national coach Pullela Gopichand is planning for the road ahead.
With the Asian Games in Japan looming, Gopichand emphasised on a tailored, highly professional approach for the Indian contingent, backed by specialised coaching units and a renewed focus on squad camaraderie.
As the focus shifts to the Asian Games, to be held in Japan from September 19-October 4, Gopichand revealed a decentralised preparation strategy to cater to the specific needs of an increasingly deep roster.
“As of now, what’s happening is that each one has a dedicated team allotted to them,” said Gopichand, confirming the specialised support for a broad group including Lakshya Sen, Ayush Shetty, Kidambi Srikanth, PV Sindhu, Unnati Hooda, Tanvi Sharma, and Devika Sihag.
“They are all now in a stage of their career where they are professional. They have a team to work with. Some of them are playing tournaments like the China Open... so we get back to work.”
Gopichand also expects the squad’s collective spirit to be a driving force, drawing parallels with recent team successes. “The team is really pumped up. Like the Thomas Cup, the players themselves do a lot of work to get together and build camaraderie. That is what we are hoping for.”
Gayatri and Treesa’s path to the podium was built on clear tactical adjustments, a testament to specific training blocks implemented over the past month-and-a-half.
“Whatever we’ve worked on in the last six weeks has helped, and it’s good to see when the practice you do actually gives you dividends on the court,” Gopichand said.
“It’s a revelation how Treesa kept charging at the net and started taking control. Gayatri’s backcourt has been good, and the rhythm on her serve was very good. These two aspects, at the crucial moments, they were able to pull through.”
Addressing their semi-final defeat against the Chinese world No.1 Liu Sheng Shu and Tan Ning, Gopichand highlighted the heavy influence of the service situation and the difficult conditions.
“They were serving very well because there was a good amount of spin and tumble on the serve. What happens is the moment you push it, the next return is very fast, and then you are engaging in the parallel game,” he said.
“When you are under a three-point deficit, it becomes very difficult to be calm and execute the strategy of lifting the first serve and counter-attacking. But you can’t run away from when people push the pace. You have to get into it.”
Asked about the emotion of watching his daughter, Gayatri, secure a World Championships medal, the coach was stoic as usual.
“I don’t know if I can articulate it in that sense. Whenever my players have played, I’ve always had the same feeling, and there’s no extra for that,” he said, adding he was “very proud of her performance and results, the way she has conducted herself, and the hard work she has done.”
While women’s doubles provided a historic high, the singles campaigns yielded mixed results. Gopichand expressed sympathy for PV Sindhu’s early exit but remained optimistic about her trajectory.
“Sindhu’s match was a bit too close. It’s a bit unfortunate she lost the way she did. But going back to her Japan Open win and her performance here, she’s definitely doing very well,” said the 52-year-old.
He praised rising talent Ayush Shetty. Asked about Lakshya Sen’s struggle, after the India men’s No.1 lost in the second round, he said: “This tournament was bad, unfortunately. I don’t specifically know what the reasons were in that sense.”
With India having now secured World Championship medals in men’s and women’s singles as well as men’s and women’s doubles, mixed doubles remains a glaring omission. Gopichand likened the situation to the step-by-step evolution of Indian badminton over the past 15 years.
“When Saina won for the first time in 2008, the question was ‘Where are the men?’ Then it was ‘Where is men’s doubles?’ and ‘Where is women’s doubles?’ We are ticking one box at a time, and hopefully, mixed doubles will be the next.”

title: Manchester United humiliated by Hull in dismal start to Premier League season
content:
Manchester United humiliated by Hull in dismal start to Premier League season
Manchester United crashed to a humiliating 2-0 defeat at promoted Hull.
Manchester United crashed to a humiliating 2-0 defeat at promoted Hull on Saturday in a dismal start to their Premier League campaign.
Michael Carrick's side were rocked by first-half goals from Semi Ajayi and Noble Mendy at the MKM Stadium.
Hull, who are back in the Premier League for the first time since 2017, were without 10 players due to injury but still put woeful United to the sword with a vibrant display.
Deep Dive
It was a chastening opening to the new season for United, who are expected to mount a title challenge after finishing third last term.
There was scant evidence that United are capable of going toe to toe with champions Arsenal on a dispiriting afternoon on Humberside.
Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos were anonymous in their United debuts in midfield after joining from Aston Villa and Chelsea, respectively.
Carrick laughed off claims that United have been handed an easy start to the season, with their trip to Hull followed by a home game against Ipswich, another of the promoted teams.
The United manager's caution proved prescient.
Former England captain Alan Shearer summed up United's malaise with a damning verdict.
"Man United have been shocking, no hunger, they've been terrible," the BBC pundit said.
Carrick's steady demeanour during his interim spell after Ruben Amorim's turbulent reign played a major role in United's revival last season.
But, now installed as permanent boss, Carrick is expected to mount a challenge for United's first English title since 2013, adding a layer of pressure he did not have to endure last season.
Carrick has been asking for more signings, and United have agreed a deal for Brighton midfielder Carlos Baleba.
He will be demanding even more after this wretched performance.
Last season, Hull became the first team to finish sixth in the Championship and earn promotion via the play-offs since Blackpool in 2010.
Tigers boss Sergej Jakirovic had insisted this week that Hull could prove the doubters wrong after a host of pundits wrote them off as relegation certainties.
Toothless United
Even Jakirovic must have been pinching himself to make sure he wasn't dreaming during Hull's first win over United since 2017.
Initially, United were on top, and Luke Shaw's cross reached Bryan Mbeumo for a fierce strike that was repelled by Hull's debutant keeper Konstantinos Tzolakis.
United threatened again moments later when Noussair Mazraoui picked out Matheus Cunha for a low drive that Tzolakis saved at full stretch.
But Hull served notice they could trouble United as Ryan Giles' cross found Oli McBurnie for a header that forced a good stop from Senne Lammens.
United's defensive vulnerability at set-pieces was brutally exposed in the 17th minute.
McBurnie easily evaded sloppy marking at a Hull corner and drilled a strike that Lammens could only push out to Nigeria defender Ajayi, who gleefully poked home from close range.
Hull's first Premier League goal for nine years sparked wild celebrations all around the MKM Stadium as orange and black-clad fans danced in delight.
Patrick Dorgu squandered a golden opportunity to silence the Hull supporters, scuffing his shot wide from Harry Maguire's pass.
United were toothless in attack and in disarray at the back.
Hull pounced to double their lead in the 38th minute.
Regan Slater's pinpoint free-kick wasn't dealt with by United's shambolic defence, and Senegal defender Mendy thumped his header past Lammens.
Taunted by chants of "you're getting mauled by the Tigers", Carrick looked shell-shocked on the touchline.
Carrick sent on Marcus Rashford at half-time, but the England forward, who spent last season on loan at Barcelona, was unable to trigger a United revival.
Hull remained the more potent force, and Mohamed Belloumi fizzed a drive just wide from distance.
Tielemans and Santos were both hauled off midway through the second half, but it made no difference as United tamely surrendered.

title: India all but out of the semi-finals race after losing to Netherlands in Men's Hockey World Cup
content:
India all but out of the semi-finals race after losing to Netherlands in Men's Hockey World Cup
India lost 1-3 against the Netherlands in the Men's Hockey World Cup on Saturday.
India are all but out of the Hockey World Cup semi-finals race after losing to the Netherlands in the Group E encounter on Saturday. The Indian contingent now needs a major miracle if they are to have any shot at reaching the last four. The side coached by Craig Fulton held the Dutch to a stalemate till the half-time, but it was only a matter of time before the Netherlands broke the deadlock, and that moment came in the third quarter. India did manage to peg one goal back, but it wasn't enough, and in the end, the hosts registered a 3-1 victory at the Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen.
India would be knocked out of the semi-finals race on Saturday itself if England beat Argentina or the contest between the two teams ends in a draw. However, the side would stay alive if the Argentine defeat the English. Even if the results go India's way, the team would still be required to win by a big margin against Argentina on Monday.
For the Netherlands, Duco Telgenkamp, Tjep Hoedemakers, and Thijs van Dam got their names on the scoring sheet, while India's lone goal came through a physically-struggling Harmanpreet Singh, who converted from a penalty corner.
Also Read: IND vs NED Highlights, Hockey World Cup
Throughout the contest, the Netherlands were the better team, and the result reflected both teams' performances on the big day. The match between the two teams was pretty neck-and-neck for the first three quarters, but the fourth and final quarter showed the gulf between India and the Netherlands, as the latter absolutely ran away with the game.
Format of World Cup
The tournament did away with the traditional quarter-final stage. The teams finishing in the top two positions in each opening pool advanced to new crossover pools, with the top two from Pools E and F progressing directly to the semi-finals.
India qualified for the second stage after finishing second in Pool D behind England. However, because England had beaten India 4-2 in the opening phase, England carried three points into Pool E while India entered without any points.
Because of no carryover points, India were in desperate need of a win against the Dutch, but in the end, it wasn't meant to be. Earlier in the group stage, India defeated Wales and Pakistan but lost to England.

title: ‘This is just the start’: Treesa-Gayatri take pride in historic World Championships bronze after semi-final defeat
content:
‘This is just the start’: Treesa-Gayatri take pride in historic World Championships bronze after semi-final defeat
Indian duo Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand secure bronze at BWF World Championships, marking India's continued success in women's doubles.
The atmosphere inside the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium on Saturday evening was electric. It was pulsating with the noise being made by the boisterous 8,000-strong crowd, hopes rising as the Indian women’s doubles pair of Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand put on a brilliant early fight in the semi-finals.
The pair had already enjoyed a slice of history, assuring themselves of bronze which extended India’s run of winning at least one medal in the BWF World Championships, since the historic first women’s doubles bronze clinched by Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa in 2011.
Their sensational run even raised hopes of continuing in as an exciting semi-final unfolded. The decibel levels soared when they pulled off the first game against China’s Liu Shen Shu and Tan Ning, but the top seeds re-set and turned the tables as the Indians lost 21-18, 13-21, 8-21.
Standing across the net from the 39th-ranked Indians was the ultimate test as the Chinese were the world No.1 pair and defending champions as well. Treesa and Gayatri had already scripted a fairytale through the week, ousting three seeded pairs.
This matchup was a different beast, but their performance on Saturday showed their potential to raise their level to match the current world beating pairs. This bronze could well be the launchpad for higher achievements.
The chasm in rankings was barely evident early on as Treesa and Gayatri matched the aggression of their opponents in the first game. Playing a fearless brand of badminton, they took a 7-2 lead. The world No.1 pair though found their footing as they reeled off 10 consecutive points.
Treesa and Gayatri though were full of resilience. Trailing 16-18, they smartly and patiently built the rallies and finished them, their five-point streak handing them the game and sending the crowd into a frenzy. “We were a bit more confident in the first game,” Gayatri said later.
The second game though proved a gruelling physical and mental contest. It was all level as Treesa and Gayatri edged 12-11 ahead. The turning point arrived moments later in the form of a 49-shot rally at 12-all. The Indians threw everything at their opponents, but Liu and Tan’s impenetrable defence absorbed the pressure, eventually winning the point.
That exchange shifted the tectonic plates of the match. A slight lapse in focus from the home favourites, and errors seeping in, allowed the Chinese to reel off eight straight points, dragging the contest into a decider. “In the second game, they played very patiently. We couldn’t match,” added Gayatri, whose father and chief national coach Pullela Gopichand was an animated figure on the sideline as he guided them through the tough contest.
The Chinese disrupted the Indians’ flow, which led to hesitation. “After the second game, the few mistakes made us a little un-confident, a little bit doubtful about the strokes that we were playing,” said Gayatri.
Also Read: Real Madrid snatch late win at Espanyol on Mourinho's return
The Indian pair retreated into a shell, becoming more defensive and losing the sting of the first game, which no pair can afford against Liu and Tan.
By the third game, Liu and Tan’s championship pedigree was on full display. They utilised clever net play and brilliant jump smashes to dictate the tempo. An exhausting 56-shot rally, the longest of the match, at 2-all in the decider seemed to drain the remaining reserves of the Indian pair.
Despite the loss, the overriding emotion for Treesa and Gayatri was pride. Ultimately, what came together here was a campaign that will be remembered for sheer tenacity. Entering the tournament having played relatively few matches this year due to an ankle injury Treesa suffered in April, it made the journey to the podium memorable.
“If you see the whole week, it has been amazing,” Treesa said. “We created many upsets. It’s such a great week for us. So many great matches, so many things to take away.”
The bronze secures their place in an elite club of Indian players who have excelled at the World Championships. The timing couldn’t be better, riding the wave of happiness after their recent inclusion in the Arjuna award list.
“Being in that club, I feel so happy,” Gayatri said. “There is a long journey ahead. I feel like this is just the start. We just need to take this in a positive and confident way. Even the Arjuna award this week also gave us some boost.” Both are 23, and can look forward to building on this effort.
Before focusing on that bright future, there was a much-needed celebration on the agenda. It wouldn’t be extravagant, just a quiet moment of gratitude with the team behind their incredible success.
“First of all, I would like to thank the team behind us,” Gayatri said. “We will take them (out) for lunch.”
And what about a personal treat to celebrate the history they had just made? “Yes,” Treesa laughed. “I will have ice-cream.”
It was a sweet, fitting end to a bittersweet day, one where a loss on the court still resulted in a legacy defining victory for Indian badminton.

title: Echoes of 2011: The Jwala-Ashwini medal that started a tradition
content:
Echoes of 2011: The Jwala-Ashwini medal that started a tradition
Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand won bronze at the BWF World Championships, ending a 15-year drought for Indian women's doubles badminton
When Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand smashed their way to guarantee themselves a BWF World Championships medal, they ended a 15-year wait in Indian badminton.
Not since August 2011 had an Indian women’s doubles pair stood on the podium. That benchmark was set by Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa, the pair not only ending a 28-year medal drought for India (after Prakash Padukone’s bronze in 1983) but kick-started the streak of India returning with at least one medal from every World Championships since.
As a new generation claims the spotlight, the pioneers reflected on a campaign that defied the odds and silenced critics in an era when their discipline was heavily marginalised. On Saturday, Treesa and Gayatri finished with bronze, India’s lone medal of the 2026 championships, after losing to China’s world No.1 pair Liu Shen Shu and Tan Ning 21-18, 13-21, 8-21 in the semi-finals.
Heading into the 2011 tournament in London, expectation from the Indian pairing was almost non-existent. Jwala, playing both women’s and mixed doubles (with V Diju), felt the weight of the challenge, yet the pair quietly plotted their ascent.
“There were no expectations from us even though we won gold at the 2010 Commonwealth Games in New Delhi,” Jwala told HT. “When we won, it was actually a big shocker for everyone. It was tough back then to block everything and perform. We won a medal in women’s doubles which was unheard of back then. You couldn’t even dream of it.”
For Ashwini, the focus was laser sharp on a formidable second-round clash against Chinese Taipei’s world No.2 pair Cheng Wen-hsing and Chien Yu-chin. Jwala had convinced her younger partner that it was “doable”, and overcoming that hurdle unlocked their path to podium.
“Getting past the second seeded pair gave us a lot of confidence going into the rounds ahead,” Ashwini told HT. “Looking back, the World Championships has always been a very fond memory for me. We not only played well, but the entire journey... I had a wonderful time, enjoyed every single bit of it, which is what makes that medal a lot more special.”
Though the unseeded Indian combine had an easy opening outing against Americans Eva Lee and Paula Lynn, overcoming Cheng and Chien was the biggest upset of the tournament. That set the path for Jwala and Ashwini to beat Hong Kong’s 11th seeds Tse Ying Suet and Poon Lok Yan in Round 3 and Indonesian 12th seeds Vita Marissa and Nadya Melati in the quarters.
They lost in the semis to Chinese fifth seeds Tian Qing and Zhao Yunlei, but only after confirming India’s first World Championships medal in 28 years.
The Indian badminton landscape was vastly different then. Women’s doubles faced existential threats within the sport, critics labelled the rallies “long and boring”, and the event was even dropped from the Indian Badminton League in 2013 in favour of a second men’s singles match.
“My medal holds a lot of weight. I have played in very strange times when they wanted to eliminate women’s doubles,” says Jwala.
“I am glad modern players are getting what we didn’t. Now badminton has better facilities, equipment, food, knowledge, and awareness. I’m happy that I was able to set a standard, a benchmark. I am going to be proud of it and no one can take that away.”
The Jwala-Ashwini breakthrough altered the nation’s trajectory on the global stage.
“It’s nice to look back and see how that medal was the start of India winning a medal back-to-back... at every single World Championships since,” Ashwini reflected on the streak. “I can’t believe it’s been 15 years since we won the medal, and now Gayatri and Treesa are assured (of a medal).”
With Treesa and Gayatri carrying the baton, the foundation laid in London has never looked stronger.

title: What happened to Ed Oliver's 2-year-old son? Tragic details of drowning surface from Bills player's family home
content:
What happened to Ed Oliver's 2-year-old son? Tragic details of drowning surface from Bills player's family home
Ed Oliver is reportedly mourning the death of his 2-year-old son, who allegedly drowned in June. The Bills DT is asking for privacy and prayers.
On Saturday evening, as the Buffalo Bills prepares for their game against the Cleveland Brown, defensive tackle Ed Oliver is reportedly still unavailable. In fact, the 28-year-old has missed multiple practice sessions lately and will likely not be in the squad for
The defensive end is reportedly not out due injury, despite the Bills suggesting he is. Reports say his two-year-old son has died in a drowning accident back in June, leaving the defensive tackle's family shattered.
According to unverified reports on social media, the defensive tackle's two-year-old son died in a drowning accident in Oliver Huffman's home in Texas. The claim seems to have originated in rumors accounts. Total Pro Sports also reported on the rumors noting that there is no confirmation.
Also read: Why is Josh Allen not playing today vs Browns? Is he injured? Reason revealed
But, as of now, neither Ed Oliver nor his family has released a statement on the tragedy, despite it being allegedly more than a month since the incident happened.
NFL Network reporter Cameron Wolfe reported later that a source close to Ed Oliver has confirmed that he is indeed mourning the loss of his son.
"Bills defensive tackle Ed Oliver and his family have been mourning the tragic loss of his son, and he is asking, per a source close to him, for “privacy and prayers at this very difficult time.'" he wrote.
What Happened To Ed Oliver's Son? What We Know And What We Don't
Joe Brady, the head coach of the Buffalo Bills, had previously attributed Ed Oliver's absence to injuries. Though, it was never specified what injury the 28-year-old was dealing with.
Also read: Trump aide Natalie Harp reacts to ‘human printer’ tag amid security clearance concerns
But the viral posts have fueled speculation, leaving many Buffalo Bills fans worried. There have also been videos circulating on social media allegedly showing Ed Oliver speaking to officers after the incident. Rumors claim that Ed Oliver was present at the address when the incident took place.
Tony Farmer, an independent journalist, claimed that there is a "media blackout" on the story of the 2-year-old's death. According to him, homicide detectives are involved in the case. He also claims that the Bills writers are aware of the story but have been refraining from breaking it.
Bills GM Releases Statement
“On behalf of the entire Buffalo Bills organization, we want to publicly express our condolences to Ed Oliver and his family on the devastating loss of his son,” Bills General Manager Brandon Beane said in a statement. “It's an unthinkable tragedy for any parent. We will continue to support Ed and his family as we all grieve this tragic loss.”

title: Treesa Jolly-Gayatri Gopichand take bronze after going down in semi-finals of BWF World Championships
content:
Treesa Jolly-Gayatri Gopichand take bronze after going down in semi-finals of BWF World Championships
The Indian pair of Treesa Jolly-Gayatri Gopichand took home bronze after going down in the semi-finals of the BWF World Championships.
Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand Pullela put up a performance to remember at the BWF World Championships, but their glorious run came to an end in the semifinal, and they took home a bronze medal. The Indian pair, the only ones to win a medal for the country in this edition of the World Championships, went down fighting against top seeds Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning, losing 21-18, 12-21, 8-21 in a hard-fought three-game battle.
Treesa and Gayatri started the game on a positive note, taking a 3-0 lead with a jam-packed crowd firmly behind them. It was the kind of atmosphere many had been craving as the Indira Gandhi Arena erupted with claps and roars, giving the Indian pair a huge psychological boost. Every point was being greeted with deafening cheers, making it feel like India had an extra edge on court.
This World Championships has been a story of Treesa and Gayatri overcoming one hurdle after another, but the semifinal arguably presented their biggest challenge yet. Standing in their way were top seeds Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning, the world No. 1 pair.
The first game saw the Indians take an early lead and create some breathing space, but the Chinese pair were in no mood to let them settle. A quick turnaround saw Liu and Tan fight back from 2-7 down to level the score at 7-7. They carried that momentum into the interval, taking an 11-7 lead.
But Treesa and Gayatri have not come this far by giving up easily, and once again, they displayed their fighting spirit. The Indian pair came out firing after the break, slowly eating into the deficit before drawing level at 12-12. The comeback underlined their belief that they could push the world No. 1 pair all the way.
The intensity of the clash kept rising, with Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand refusing to be tamed by the top-seeded Chinese pair. The Indians kept pushing, matching Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning point for point as the first game moved towards its business end.
With the score locked at 18-18, the pressure was immense, and every rally felt like it could decide the game. Then came the defining moment. Treesa and Gayatri produced three points on the trot to move from 18-18 to 21-18 and seal the opening game. The Indira Gandhi Arena erupted as the fans jumped off their seats, roaring their approval.
The second game began with the Chinese pair knowing they had their backs against the wall, and they came out swinging, taking the opening point with a powerful smash. But the ice-and-fire combination of Treesa and Gayatri was ready for the challenge. After dropping the early points, the Indians fought back to make it 4-5 and stayed right in the contest.
Gayatri began targeting the Chinese pair's backhand, finding success with the tactic and putting them under pressure. However, Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning quickly read the change in approach and adjusted their game, stretching their lead once again.
But there were levels to this contest, and Treesa and Gayatri kept raising theirs, feeding off the energy inside the packed Indira Gandhi Arena. It was once again a neck-and-neck battle, with neither side willing to take its foot off the gas. The rallies grew longer, and the pressure kept building, before India edged ahead 11-10 at the halfway mark, taking a crucial psychological advantage.
The rotation was clearly visible in their movements as Treesa and Gayatri tried to keep their opponents guessing. But there was a reason Liu and Tan were the top seeds. The net game began to hurt India in the second half, with a string of unforced errors allowing the Chinese pair to open up an 18-12 lead. Treesa and Gayatri kept finding the net and also sent crucial shots wide, handing away valuable points. The Indians could not recover from the setback and eventually lost the second game 13-21, with the momentum firmly shifting towards Liu/Tan.
The final game started on an even footing, with both pairs trading points early on. But Liu and Tan soon found a way to adapt to the Indian pair’s game, and once they did, they began pulling away. Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand Pullela struggled to find answers as the Chinese pair took an 11-5 lead at the halfway mark.
The second half proved even tougher for the Indians, who found it increasingly difficult to hold their nerves against a pair that kept tightening the pressure. Every point slipped away painfully, and the disappointment was visible on Treesa and Gayatri’s faces as they realised the silver was moving further out of reach. They eventually lost the final game 8-21. It was a heartbreaking end, but there was no denying the glorious run they had put together.

title: From a shy girl to team mentor, Savita Punia says hockey changed her life
content:
From a shy girl to team mentor, Savita Punia says hockey changed her life
Amstelveen, There was a time when Savita Punia needed her mother to stand at the doorstep whenever she would step out of the house, too hesitant to speak to seniors in the Indian hockey team, and uncomfortable facing the camera.
Today, the veteran goalkeeper travels across the world, speaks confidently and mentors the young women hockey players.
The 36-year-old Savita, who is the most experienced player in the FIH World Cup with 317 caps, is only four matches away from breaking the Indian record for playing most matches , currently held by the veteran goalkeeper Vandana Katariya.
While looking back at her glorious career, Savita feels hockey has changed her as a person too.
"When I started playing, I couldn't talk to my seniors much beyond saying 'good morning', but today I'm a team mentor. My confidence has grown significantly. I've learned to speak while playing hockey." she told PTI in an exclusive interview.
"I often share my journey with the young players. Today, players are learning these things very quickly. It took us a long time to grow," said the veteran who is often called the wall of Indian Hockey.
"It wouldn't be wrong to say that hockey has completely changed me. There was a time when I was afraid to even leave the house alone. Even if I had to go to my uncle's house in the neighbourhood, I would ask my mother to stand at the door. But today, I can travel to any corner of the world alone," she said.
Reflecting on her past, Savita recalled a time when she seriously considered quitting hockey for being upset by the rude behaviour of a roadways bus conductor.
"It was in 2011, when I was returning home from camp, and at that time, there was no transport available. I had my luggage along with my goalkeeping bag. Bus services were very limited in the evening, and because of my luggage, they refused to let me board the bus. The conductor suggested buying two tickets, but I felt I couldn't afford five hundred rupees." she said.
"He then said, 'You're a girl, if you call out once, ten boys will come'. I started crying and told my father that I didn't want to play hockey anymore. My father then bought a second-hand car so I could continue."
Indian goalkeepers Savita and Bichoo Devi are receiving considerable praise at this World Cup, but the former said that it was not the case in the past.
"The status that goalkeepers have achieved in India wasn't easy. Previously, people would only ask after matches who scored the goals, not who saved them. There was a mindset that if someone was unfit, slow, or not healthy, they would be made the goalkeeper. Now, times have changed."
"Becoming a goalkeeper was the best decision of my life. I want to be remembered as a good goalkeeper and a good mentor."
When asked about her role in the team, she said that the focus is on keeping the atmosphere positive.
"As seniors, our focus is on maintaining a good team atmosphere. The players listen to me, and I feel happy when something good comes out of it. Navneet, Neha, Salima, Sushila, Lalremsiami, all the senior players are working towards it and we always talk about taking this team one step further." she said.
Savita, who has seen many ups and downs in Indian women's hockey, said that the disappointment of missing out on a medal at the Tokyo Olympics has become an inspiration for the players.
"No one in Tokyo expected the Indian women's hockey team to perform so well. Everyone praised us, but the lack of a medal left us with a sense of regret," Savita said.
"Since then, we have worked hard individually and as a team. That inspired us, and if we play to our strengths, we can move one step forward," said the second female hockey player to be awarded the Padma Shri.
When asked about the future, Savita said that her current goals are the World Cup and the Asian Games, and she is not thinking beyond that.
"I like to improve myself every day. Right now, the World Cup and Asian Games are very important, and I'll focus on them. After that, we'll see what's next," she said.
When asked what message she would like to give to players who are about to pick up a hockey stick for the first time, she said, "I would tell parents to support their children. Sports in India are growing rapidly, and so is hockey."
"Today, there are tournaments like the Senior and Junior Nationals, Khelo India, and Hockey India League, so train with that in mind."
"But dedication, commitment, and discipline are essential for this. If you work hard, you can achieve anything. If you hear the stories of not just me, but many players in the team, you might wonder if it's really possible. But if you work hard, everything is possible."

title: Shubhankar makes cut after spectacular ace at Nexo Championship
content:
Shubhankar makes cut after spectacular ace at Nexo Championship
Aberdeenshire , Shubhankar Sharma ended his streak of four missed cuts as he made the weekend rounds at the Nexo Championship here.
He produced the shot of the day with a spectacular hole-in-one on the sixth hole during an even-par second round.
Shubhankar, who opened with a 73 on Thursday, followed it with a 72 to reach one-over 145 after 36 holes and was tied 22 and comfortably made the weekend rounds at Trump International Golf Links.
The other Indian in the field, Yuvraj Sandhu , missed the cut.
Starting his second round from the first tee, Shubhankar opened with a birdie before dropping a shot at the fifth. He then delivered the highlight of his round at the par-three sixth, holing his tee shot for a sensational ace.
The Indian subsequently picked up birdies at the 12th and 13th, but his progress was checked by bogeys at the ninth, 11th, 15th, and 16th. He eventually signed for a level-par 72.
The ace was particularly significant for Shubhankar, who has endured a difficult stretch on the DP World Tour. The weekend appearance gives the two-time DP World Tour winner an opportunity to build momentum and climb the leaderboard over the final 36 holes.
At the top, England's Matthew Southgate took a one-stroke lead into the weekend after a second straight two-under 70 moved him to four-under for the tournament.
Southgate, who started the day three shots off the lead, negotiated the testing and windy conditions in Aberdeenshire with a disciplined round.
He made a birdie at the 17th before dropping his only shot of the day at the sixth. A chip-in eagle at the seventh provided the decisive moment and lifted him into outright first.
Matthew Jordan, who finished runner-up in Denmark last week, carded a three-under 69 to share second place at three-under with South African Shaun Norris, who also shot 69.
Also tied at second were Scotland's Scott Jamieson and overnight leader Marcus Kinhult.

title: Jenny Simpson health scare: World champion runner forced to retire due to this rare disease; What is ARVC?
content:
Jenny Simpson health scare: World champion runner forced to retire due to this rare disease; What is ARVC?
Jenny Simpson experienced cardiac arrest from ARVC in June and announced she won't return to competitive running.
Jenny Simpson, world champion runner, has disclosed that a rare heart condition led to her cardiac arrest during a race in June, and she has confirmed that she will not be returning to competitive running.
In an Instagram post on Thursday, the 39-year-old athlete stated that she was diagnosed with Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), which resulted in "dangerous heart rhythms that ultimately caused my heart to stop."
She mentioned that the diagnosis means that going back to running could be hazardous. “That chapter has ended. Thankfully, my story hasn't.”
What is ARVC?
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is a rare condition that poses a significant risk of life-threatening abnormal heart rhythms, Cleveland Clinic reported. The majority of individuals affected by this disorder possess a genetic variation. Timely diagnosis and intervention are crucial, allowing your healthcare provider to assist you in preventing irregular heart rhythms through medications and procedures.
ARVC affects approximately 1 in every 2,000 to 1 in every 5,000 individuals. While it frequently occurs within families, it can also manifest in individuals without any family history of the condition.
Also Read: Who is Nneka Ogwumike? Los Angeles Sparks forward announces retirement after 15 WNBA season
Jenny Simpson fainted, administered CPR on the track
Simpson fainted while walking among a group of girls during a mile run at an event in Raleigh, North Carolina. She was administered CPR on the track, and an automated external defibrillator was utilized before medical staff transported her to the hospital.
The Sir Walter Running Team released a statement on Instagram soon after Simpson's collapse, thanking the medical personnel for their prompt response at the event.
"We are incredibly grateful to the individuals who responded immediately, as well as EMS and the medical professionals who handled the situation with such care, urgency, and professionalism," the statement said.
“Jenny is receiving excellent medical care, and our thoughts are with her and her family during this time,” it added.
'I'm still here,' says Jenny Simpson
Contemplating her emotions following the troubling event, Simpson said: "You might be wondering what would be the right thing to say to me after an event like this. Please do not say that you're sorry or that you feel bad for me. If it is true in your heart, please tell me you're glad that I'm here. That's how I feel — so glad that I'm still here."
For nearly ten years beginning in 2007, Simpson was recognized as the most accomplished female 1,500-meter runner in the United States. She secured the world championship title in 2011, achieved second place at the world championships on two occasions, and earned a bronze medal at the Rio Olympics in 2016.
